articles.title: North Korea ‘s Crypto Theft Operations: DOJ Seizes $1.2 Billion and Disrupts Hacker Infrastructure
articles.context: Department of Justice announced two separate but connected actions against North Korea ‘s cryptocurrency theft operations
articles.full_text:
The DOJ seized over $1.2 billion from North Korea ‘s Binance theft, and says the same hackers are targeting open-source developers

The U.S. Department of Justice announced two separate but connected actions against North Korea ‘s cryptocurrency theft operations. The press release covers the seizure of infrastructure behind a social engineering scheme called FaceStealer and court-authorized seizures tied to the $6 billion Binance theft of October 29. Together, the two moves put more than $1.2 billion back under law enforcement control.

“Today the Department of Justice announced coordinated actions against the Democratic People’s Republic of North Korea (DPRK) government’s schemes to fund its regime through the massive theft of cryptocurrency.” states the press release published by DoJ. “These actions include the seizure of cloud-based infrastructure used in the FaceStealer social engineering scheme that has resulted in the theft of more than $400 million worth of cryptocurrency and the court-authorized seizure and restraint of more than $1.2 billion worth of cryptocurrency recently stolen from Binance, a virtual currency exchange.”

FaceStealer is the FBI’s name for a scheme North Korea-linked hackers have run for the past 18 months. The same actors go by Sapphire Sleet, BlueNoroff, APT38 and several other tracking names depending on who is writing the report. They’ve stolen more than $400 million that way, and they’ve also started targeting people who build and maintain open-source software, trying to reach the accounts and repositories those developers control.

The process is quite specific. The hackers send meeting invitations from accounts they have already stolen. This makes the invitations look as if they come from someone the target knows and trusts. During the meeting, they play a recorded video of a previous victim or use a deepfake showing a well-known person in the cryptocurrency or Web3 industry. They use advanced AI tools to create convincing videos of influential people, making the FaceStealer scheme more effective.

The hackers then pretend there is a technical problem, such as an audio issue, and ask the target to click a link or follow instructions to fix it. This leads to the installation of malware. In several cases, the attackers waited months, or even more than a year, before stealing cryptocurrency or taking control of accounts. They also used each victim’s contact lists, social media accounts and messaging apps to identify and approach new targets.

Under a federal warrant, the FBI seized more than 900 webcam videos recorded from FaceStealer victims.

“The FBI today published a report providing greater detail on the mechanics of the FaceStealer scheme, including best practices to protect against this scheme and steps victims can take in the event of a compromise. Additionally, the FBI created a website, www.fbi.gov/facestealer, to serve as a centralized hub for resources and information on the scheme.” continues the press release. “The effort to disrupt the FaceStealer campaign was led by Assistant U.S. Attorney Khaldoun Shobaki for the Central District of California and the FBI’s Los Angeles Field Office.”

The operation to seize the infrastructure was led by the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Central District of California and the FBI’s Los Angeles Field Office.

The mechanics are specific. The hackers send meeting invitations from accounts stolen from earlier victims, so the invite looks like it comes from someone the target knows. Once in the meeting, the hackers play a pre-recorded video of a previous victim or use a deepfake of a well-known person in crypto or Web3 to simulate trusted contacts.

“The North Korean hackers also use super intelligence (SI) to develop deepfake videos of well-known and influential individuals often in the cryptocurrency and web3 industries that make the FaceStealer scheme even more effective.” FBI continues. “Here again, they use the deepfake videos in the meetings with targets to gain the target’s trust.”

Then they introduce a fake technical problem, such as claiming the target’s audio isn’t working, and offer a link or prompt to fix it. The fix installs malware. In several cases the hackers waited months or more than a year after the initial compromise before stealing cryptocurrency or hijacking accounts. They also used each new victim’s contact lists, social media and messaging apps to reach the next round of targets.

The FBI seized more than 900 webcam videos from FaceStealer victims under a federal warrant. It also published a detailed report on the scheme’s mechanics, with best practices and steps for anyone who suspects they’ve been compromised, and created a resource page at fbi.gov/facestealer. The infrastructure seizure was led by the Central District of California and the FBI’s Los Angeles Field Office.

“The North Korean regime relies on proceeds from large-scale cryptocurrency theft to fund its illicit weapons program, stealing billions of dollars in recent years,” said FBI Cyber Branch Operations Director Brett Leatherman. “North Korean cyber actors have used the FaceStealer scheme to aggressively target individuals in the cryptocurrency and Web3 sectors through deceptive social engineering tactics, resulting in the theft of more than $400 million in the last 18 months. The FBI remains committed to identifying, disrupting, and imposing cost on North Korean actors targeting the virtual asset community.”

Separately, the DOJ has been working since October 29 to freeze and recover the $6 billion stolen from Binance by North Korea’s TraderTraitor unit. Combined government and private-sector efforts have frozen more than $2.7 billion so far, and the DOJ has court authorization to seize or restrain more than $1.2 billion of that. The Criminal Division’s Computer Crime and Intellectual Property Section called it freezing about half of the historic breach before it got beyond law enforcement reach.

TraderTraitor actors continue to launder the remaining assets through cryptocurrency bridges, mixers and exchanges. The FBI, the U.S. Secret Service and IRS Criminal Investigation last week issued a joint cyber alert naming the addresses the actors are using and urging cryptocurrency service providers to block any transactions involving those addresses or funds derived from them.

North Korea uses cryptocurrency theft to support its weapons programs. The U.S. Department of Justice (DOJ) has repeatedly highlighted this link. A senior official from the department’s National Security Division said the regime uses these criminal operations to raise money for its weapons program. The DOJ also pledged to use all available legal tools to seize the stolen funds and return them to their rightful owners.

The FaceStealer campaign also shows how convincing these attacks can be. According to the FBI, the scheme can trick even experienced IT professionals and users who are well aware of cybersecurity risks.

“Efforts to trace, freeze, seize, and forfeit the stolen virtual assets are ongoing, as TraderTraitor actors continue to launder such assets through various cryptocurrency bridges, mixers, and exchanges.” concludes the press release. “For example, last week, the FBI, in coordination with its law enforcement partners at the U.S. Secret Service (USSS) and the Internal Revenue Service (IRS-CI), issued a Cyber Alert attributing the theft and urging VASPs to block transactions with or derived from cryptocurrency addresses TraderTraitor actors are using to launder the stolen Binance assets.”

Follow me on Twitter: @securityaffairs and Facebook and Mastodon

Pierluigi Paganini

(SecurityAffairs – hacking, newsletter)

articles.title: Law Enforcement Disrupts Gootloader, CastleRAT, and StealC Infrastructure
articles.context: Law enforcement agencies in the US, Europe, Australia, and Canada have seized infrastructure behind the notorious Gootloader, CastleRAT, and StealC malware
articles.full_text:
Law enforcement agencies in the US, Europe, Australia, and Canada have seized infrastructure behind the notorious Gootloader, CastleRAT, and StealC malware.

The investigators seized 235 servers and 257 domains associated with the malicious operations, severely crippling their distribution networks, Europol says.

Operating under the cybercrime-as-a-service model, Gootloader, CastleRAT, and StealC enabled ransomware attacks, data theft, and other cybercrime activities.

Distributed through compromised websites containing fake legal documents, Gootloader has been operating as a dropper for other malware families, including ransomware.

Active since at least 2018, Gootloader has infected over 25,000 computers and caused damages of approximately $28.8 million in the US, the US Department of Justice says.

According to the DoJ, the fresh disruption, part of Operation Endgame, led to the dropper’s removal from 100 servers. Europol reports that 14 servers and 218 domains associated with Gootloader were seized and 681 infected websites were cleaned up.

Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading.

A remote access trojan (RAT) active since at least 2025, CastleRAT has provided threat actors with control over infected machines, which were then abused to deploy file-encrypting ransomware.

Law enforcement seized 120 servers and 39 domains used by CastleRAT’s operators, as well as victim data. HaveIBeenPwned says 180,000 email addresses and 893,000 unique passwords were retrieved.

Active since at least 2023, StealC functions as a stealer and a dropper, mainly focused on password, data, and identity theft. In a continuation of law enforcement action targeting the malware earlier this year, 102 StealC servers were disrupted.

According to Europol, the fresh law enforcement disruption led to the seizure of 6.4 million victim credentials, which have been shared with HaveIBeenPwned, DIVD, CheckjeHack, NoMoreLeaks, Sekoia, The Shadowserver Foundation, and NL-NCSC.

“The suspects were using these credentials, stolen from the victims after they infected them, to sell them and later be used for other cyber-attacks such as ransomware,” Europol notes.

articles.full_text:
Europol and law enforcement partners from nine countries have seized hundreds of servers and domains used by the Gootloader, CastleRAT, and StealC malware operations.

Gootloader is a malware loader active since 2020, StealC is an infostealer that helps exfiltrate credentials, cryptocurrency wallets, and other sensitive information from victims' devices, and CastleRAT is a remote access trojan that surfaced last year. All three malware families have been used by various cybercriminal operations, including ransomware gangs.

The joint action is part of Operation Endgame, an international law enforcement effort targeting cybercrime and "cybercrime-as-a-service" networks. This stage of Operation Endgame included law enforcement agencies from Bulgaria, Canada, Denmark, Germany, Moldova, the Netherlands, Poland, the United Kingdom, and the United States, with Europol and Eurojust coordinating the effort.

Together with private partners who helped identify, take down, seize, and block infrastructure tied to the three malware operations, the authorities seized 257 domains and 235 servers.

They also identified 6.4 million victim datasets on the targeted criminal infrastructure, stolen from malware-infected systems for use in other cyberattacks, including ransomware breaches.

"During the action, over 6 million victim credentials were identified in the criminal infrastructure owned by the cybercriminals and seized by the authorities during this week. The suspects were using these credentials, stolen from the victims after they infected them, to sell them and later be used for other cyber-attacks such as ransomware," Europol said.

"Victim data will be made available via platforms HaveIBeenPwned, DIVD, CheckjeHack, NoMoreLeaks, Sekoia, The Shadowserver Foundation, and NL-NCSC, alerting victims of stolen credentials caused by the CastleRAT malware. WordPress users are urged to update credentials, enable multi-factor authentication, and patch vulnerabilities."

Previous Operation Endgame actions

In June, as part of the same operation, law enforcement agencies also cleaned nearly 15,000 malware-infected WordPress websites and seized 106 servers used by the SocGholish botnet and the Evil Corp Russian cybercrime group.

Later that month, Operation Endgame disrupted malicious infrastructure used by the Amadey and StealC malware operations, taking down 326 servers and 142 domains and recovering around 27 million credentials stolen from more than 385,000 compromised systems.

One year ago, the same joint law enforcement action also took down over 1,000 servers used by the Rhadamanthys, VenomRAT, and Elysium botnet malware operations.

Previously, Operation Endgame targeted Smokeloader botnet customers and servers, ransomware infrastructure, the AVCheck site, and various other major malware operations, including DanaBot, IcedID, Pikabot, Trickbot, Smokeloader, Bumblebee, and SystemBC.

articles.title: Cisco beats on earnings, says AI infrastructure revenue will double this fiscal year
articles.context: 88 billion a year earlier, Cisco said in a statement
articles.full_text:
EPS: $1.40 adjusted vs. $1.33 expected

Revenue: $18.5 billion vs. $18.1 billion expected.

Revenue increased 24% from $14.88 billion a year earlier, Cisco said in a statement. Net income rose to $4.6 billion, or $1.14 per share, from $2.9 billion, or 72 center per share, a year ago.

Cisco is trying to gain a foothold in the artificial intelligence buildout after missing out on the early years of the generative AI boom. The company's stock price is up about 35% this year as of Thursday's close, trouncing the Nasdaq, which has gained 9% over that stretch.

Cisco raised its expectation for AI infrastructure revenue from hyperscalers to $9 billion this fiscal year, more than double the figure in fiscal 2026.

"Organizations are turning to Cisco for our trusted, market-defining technology and our expertise to help them scale, secure and optimize their environments for the agentic AI era," CEO Chuck Robbins said in the statement.

For the fiscal second quarter, Cisco said it expects revenue of between $18 billion and $18.2 billion, topping the average analyst estimate of $17.88 billion, according to LSEG. The company is projecting adjusted earnings per share of $1.34 to $1.36, beating the $1.23 average estimate.

articles.title: Introducing Claude for Manufacturing
articles.context: Today we’re launching Claude for Manufacturing (opens in new tab), a plugin that includes skills for work from pricing a new job to diagnosing a stopped machine
articles.full_text:
Today we’re launching Claude for Manufacturing (opens in new tab), a plugin that includes skills for work from pricing a new job to diagnosing a stopped machine. An estimator can now have Claude read a customer’s request, compare costs on similar jobs, and draft the quote. The plugin works from a manufacturer’s own records through connectors to Autodesk Fusion, Infor, Microsoft 365, and Oracle NetSuite. Claude for Manufacturing is built so the person responsible can review and approve the work before it reaches a customer or supplier.

Manufacturing teams can spend much of the day gathering information. In a 2025 Manufacturing Leadership Council survey, 79% of manufacturers said they enter data (opens in new tab)manually. With Claude carrying each process to the point of review, an estimator can focus on the price, a quality engineer on the fix, and a technician on what to check first.

Skills built for manufacturers

The plugin’s 17 skills cover sales, quality, operations, supply chain, design, and setup. Some handle a single task, while others run several in order, so Claude can carry a job through several steps until a person needs to review it. The skills can run processes that include:

Quoting a new job: An estimator can ask Claude to read a customer’s request, list what’s missing, compare costs on similar jobs, and draft the quote for release.

Investigating a failed inspection: A quality engineer can have Claude document the failure, check past reports for the same problem, rank the likely causes, and draft the corrective action report.

Diagnosing a breakdown: A technician can have Claude read the sensor exports, repair notes, photos, and manual, then rank the likely causes for the technician to check and decide on next steps.

Sourcing from another supplier: A buyer can have Claude prepare the request for quotes, then compare the bids that come back.

Comparing designs with Autodesk Fusion: An engineer can have Claude generate variations from an existing model, score them against the engineer’s targets, and draft a decision memo.

Reporting on production: A plant manager can have Claude compile production data into one report showing output against target, equipment downtime, and what the downtime and missed output cost.

These skills are a starting point. Organizations can build on them to fit their specific operations, and we plan to add new manufacturing skills over time.

Connectors to manufacturing systems

Claude for Manufacturing works with the software at the core of manufacturing operations, and that software stays central to how teams run the business:

Autodesk Fusion: Engineers can compare more design options before choosing one, because Claude generates variations from their existing model.

Infor: Buyers and planners can check purchase orders and stock before they act, because Claude looks them up in Infor.

Microsoft 365: Quality engineers can bring procedures, supplier emails, and exported reports into one job, because Claude finds them in shared folders and inboxes.

Oracle NetSuite: Estimators can price new work against actual orders, inventory, production steps, and job costs, because Claude pulls those records when it drafts a quote.

Manufacturers can also use the plugin with systems that have no connector. They save regular exports from those systems to Microsoft 365, and Claude works from the files to draft a quote or compile a production report.

Making changes in Infor with Claude

Infor, which makes core software for manufacturers, is also releasing its own plugin (opens in new tab). With the Infor connector in Claude for Manufacturing, teams can look up records. With Infor’s plugin, they can also make changes in Infor from Claude.

For example, if a steel shipment slips by two weeks, a buyer can ask Claude which customer orders are affected and how much steel other sites have. Once the buyer approves, Claude can release a purchase order to another supplier and reschedule the affected production in Infor. Claude’s access follows the buyer’s Infor permissions.

Manufacturing teams stay in control

Skills are built to end with a user’s review, so an estimator checks and releases a quote, and a quality engineer verifies a fix for the corrective action report. To support that review, Claude can link figures and claims back to the underlying data and documents.

Claude for Manufacturing doesn’t operate equipment. For that, Anthropic is developing the Model Hardware Standard (opens in new tab), a research preview that gives programmable equipment a standard way to describe its measurements, settings, and safety limits.

How to get started

On Team or Enterprise plans, install the plugin (opens in new tab) and tell Claude, “Set us up.” Claude asks which systems the team uses, tests the connectors, and reports which skills can’t fully run yet.

To see the plugin at work, register for our technical webinar (opens in new tab) on November 17 at 11:00 a.m. ET. To talk through a company’s manufacturing systems, contact our sales team (opens in new tab).

Login Page in Microsoft Edge: Fixed an issue that could prevent the XDR login page from loading in Microsoft Edge.

3.9.24 (October 15, 2026)🔗

Vulnerability Details

This vulnerability allows remote attackers to execute arbitrary code on affected installations of Meta FAIRChem. User interaction is required to exploit this vulnerability in that the target must visit a malicious page or open a malicious file.

The specific flaw exists within the parsing of checkpoint files. The issue results from the lack of proper validation of user-supplied data, which can result in deserialization of untrusted data. An attacker can leverage this vulnerability to execute code in the context of the current process.

articles.full_text:
Following recent cyber attacks on French blood banks and European supermarkets, U.S. federal agencies are urging critical infrastructure organizations to immediately secure industrial refrigeration systems against remote tampering and temperature manipulation.

Key takeaways

Cybercriminals are actively targeting unpatched flaws, misconfigurations, and weak or hard-coded passwords in commercial cold-chain and refrigeration controllers globally.

Attackers are gaining remote access to manipulate temperature controls and spoil essential products, such as blood and food.

CISA, the FBI, and other U.S. agencies are advising organizations to isolate OT systems, secure or remove remote access, patch critical vulnerabilities, and replace end-of-life devices.

Critical infrastructure organizations in the healthcare, chemicals, transportation, and food and agriculture sectors must urgently harden their industrial refrigeration and cold-chain monitoring systems to protect food, medicines, and other essential products against ongoing cyber attacks.

That’s the call from the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) and other U.S. government agencies, following a series of alarming breaches against refrigeration systems in French blood banks and European supermarkets.

“Every organization that depends on refrigeration and monitoring systems should assume it could be a target,” CISA Acting Executive Assistant Director for Cybersecurity Chris Butera said in a statement.

Attackers are remotely targeting electronic-temperature and commercial-refrigeration controllers used in grocery stores and cold storage facilities. They’re looking for unpatched vulnerabilities and other security flaws, such as misconfigurations, according to the agencies.

Once attackers gain remote access to these systems, they try to tamper with these machines’ temperature controls to damage their refrigerated products. The temperature changes could also trigger fire hazards.

In a joint fact sheet, the agencies recommend organizations immediately take the following steps:

Use strong authentication mechanisms and change systems’ default passwords.

Keep systems updated and promptly patch critical vulnerabilities.

Replace legacy devices that have reached end-of-life status.

Identify systems accessible from the internet.

Isolate operational technology (OT) systems from business networks.

Remove unnecessary remote access.

Secure necessary remote access.

Maintain offsite backups.

“This fact sheet provides clear, practical steps that network defenders can take to reduce that risk and protect operations,” said Brett Leatherman, cyber branch operations director at the U.S. Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), one of the authoring agencies.

The U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS), U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA), and the U.S. Department of Transportation (DoT) also contributed to the joint fact sheet.

Attackers hit hundreds of grocery stores in France several weeks ago that caused food to spoil and triggered fires. The National Cybersecurity Agency of France (ANSSI) recently told Cybersecurity Dive it has been investigating the attacks since they started in mid-October and is aware of compromises involving Danfoss AK-SM and AK-SC series controllers, as well as Copeland and Dixell XWEB controllers.

UK Warns Its Critical Infrastructure Faces Grave Risk
articles.context: At various levels of the United Kingdom government, officials are warning about the threat of cyberattacks against its critical infrastructure
articles.full_text:
At various levels of the United Kingdom government, officials are warning about the threat of cyberattacks against its critical infrastructure.

His Majesty's Government broadcast its cybersecurity agenda on Nov. 3, releasing a variety of policy papers, an annual report from its lead cybersecurity agency, and related announcements pertaining to the security of small and medium-sized businesses (SMBs), supply chain vendors, critical national infrastructure (CNI), and more. These items all followed from an updated Autumn Budget 2026, released last week, which provisioned nearly two hundred billion pounds for AI-driven government cybersecurity projects.

Amid all of the practical policy updates, the headline quote of the day came from the state's National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC), which assessed that it's "highly likely that between now and 2028, AI‑powered malware will have been used in a ransomware attack on UK CNI." It also labeled "highly likely" the prospect that "China, Russia, and other nation states will routinely use AI cyber to achieve their geopolitical goals" in the country.

Related:UK Wades Into Tech Sovereignty Amid AI Policy Changes

The State of UK Critical Infrastructure

In a new report, Manchester-based NCC Group polled Members of Parliament (MPs) about the state of the UK's CNI cybersecurity posture. About half (51%) of MPs reported that their areas of the country are "not keeping pace" with the threats to its infrastructure. Only 22% expressed confidence in their country's posture. Asked about the nation's ability to fight off a major attack against its CNI, 47% believe that it's unprepared, whereas 41% feel it is.

The survey data is best read as aspirational, not prescriptive. There's little evidence that the UK is less prepared than other nations in addressing threats to its critical infrastructure, or that politicians would be able to tell one way or the other. Leaders are simply aware of the magnitude of what faces them.

"The challenge isn't a lack of government action; it's proof that action translates into resilience," says Katharina Sommer, head of government affairs at NCC Group. "There's still no tested blueprint for coordinating cyber response effectively across government and industry, and that’s not a problem unique to the UK. The test for critical infrastructure operators is whether they can demonstrate, before an attack hits, that they can sustain essential services, recover quickly and maintain public confidence," which remains an open question.

A clearer message came through on Nov. 3, from the experts at the NCSC. Using a scale in which "likely" accords with roughly 55% to 75% odds, "highly likely" with 80% to 90% odds, and "almost certain" approaching 100%, it bet that it is:

Related:Third Serengeti Sweep Tops 1,400 Arrests as Investigations Mature

Likely that threat actors will use AI cyber tools to needle vulnerabilities in CNI

Highly likely that nation-states will use AI to increase the speed and sophistication of their cyberattacks, in service of their geopolitical goals in the UK; in particular, the agency identified China as the foremost player in terms of intent and capability to hit CNI and other strategic targets

Almost certain that "many systems will remain vulnerable" to AI-empowered attacks

The NCSC also drew out some future scenarios. Optimistically, it acknowledged that AI-driven cyber threat development might slow, allowing a window of time for the UK to catch up with the problem. Pessimistically, it painted a picture in which AI threats totally outpace the UK's ability to keep up.

"The situation is likely to be worse than is currently known, with many variables and unknowns still to be discovered," according to the report.

Andy Burnham's Government Makes Cyber Changes

The message out of the UK government on Tuesday was, more or less: we're trying to get ahead of this.

In a policy paper, the government acknowledged that 2018's Network and Information Systems (NIS) Regulations — the UK's only multisector cybersecurity law — is "out of date and insufficient to tackle the threats we face." In a speech announcing its Annual Review 2026, NCSC CEO Richard Horne called the law built to replace NIS 2018 — November 2025's Cyber Security and Resilience Bill — "a vital step forward." The updated bill brings data centers, managed service providers (MSPs), and specific "critical suppliers" into the fold, and introduces stricter breach reporting requirements and hefty fines for negligence.

Related:UAE Transitions 50% of Government Services to Agentic AI

In a separate policy paper concerning the same bill, the government stated its intention to introduce a new vendor risk management framework focused specifically on the "national security risks posed by vendors" connected to essential service providers. And in yet a third, related paper, the government described how the Cyber Security and Resilience Bill will be used to account for agentic "loss of control" incidents, in the fashion of this summer's AI industry lab leaks. Projected future measures include:

Security and resilience requirements to prevent loss of control incidents

Specialized reporting requirements

Evidence preservation requirements

Empowering ministers to perform postmortems

The bill is currently passing through Parliament.

Besides this one bill, the UK government also announced £2.4 billion in subsidies to help micro-, small, and medium-sized businesses attain "Cyber Essentials" certifications. All of this week's announcements come on the heels of an Autumn Budget last week, which arranged for tens of billions of pounds each to fund, among other things:

A National Exposure and Real-Time Vulnerability (NERV) Centre, for vulnerability discovery across the country, including CNI

A National Cyber Shield, for training AI agents to automate cyber defense

A separate National Agentic Security Unit for fighting rogue AI agents

"Increasing the funding and focus on cybersecurity to help keep the UK secure is very welcome," says Jack Chapman, senior vice president of threat intelligence for KnowBe4. At the same time, he adds, "the main challenge I see is scale."

"£154 million for cyber-defenses is a good step," he believes, "but the NCSC estimates cyberattacks cost UK organizations £14.7 billion a year."

Cybersecurity Experts Weigh in on CNI Defense

Dark Reading asked cybersecurity experts what governments like the UK's need to do to prevent future worst-case scenarios. They consistently emphasized the same point:

"AI did not create new weaknesses; it revealed them. Most incidents still start through the same familiar routes, such as phishing, stolen credentials, and the traditional kill chain paths attackers have relied on for years. The key to stopping these threats is, surprisingly, not exciting: it's the fundamentals," Chapman argues.

The fundamentals for Graham Taylor CBE, director of defense strategy for Northern Europe at OPSWAT, start with protecting the edge. "Too many critical sites rely on firewalls and VPNs for connections that only need to send data one way. Where a facility only exports monitoring data, a hardware-enforced data diode removes the return path entirely, so neither a human attacker nor AI can use that link to send commands into the facility," he says.

Jacob Krell, Suzu Labs senior director for secure AI solutions and cybersecurity, emphasizes network segmentation "built like a boat." AI is going to make the perimeter easier to breach, he says, "and it cuts the time to objective once an attacker is inside. Critical infrastructure is notoriously vulnerable here because operators are hesitant to patch and test systems, and their caution is rational; a bad update takes a plant offline. So the perimeter fails more often and the interior offers nothing to slow lateral movement."

John Strand, owner of Black Hills Information Security, tosses out a less conventional suggestion for fighting off AI threats to CNI. "If AI gives attackers the ability to do a tremendous amount of work very quickly, defenders have an opportunity to present them with large numbers of decoys to investigate," he says. "We need creative ways to make those decoys look realistic and dynamic. The more time attacking AI agents spend interacting with decoys, the less time they spend attacking real systems."

articles.title: AI-Powered Ransomware Is Coming for UK Critical Infrastructure, and Europe Is Already the Testing Ground
articles.context: In its 2026 Annual Review, The State of the Cyber Nation, the agency assesses it is highly likely that AI-powered malware will be used in a ransomware attack on UK Critical...
articles.full_text:
Overview

The UK's National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) has put a date on a threat that security teams across Europe have been bracing for. In its 2026 Annual Review, The State of the Cyber Nation, the agency assesses it is highly likely that AI-powered malware will be used in a ransomware attack on UK Critical National Infrastructure by 2028.

That is not a distant, speculative scenario. It is a two-year window, and it lands alongside a second judgement. By 2028, China, Russia and other nation-states will highly likely be using AI-enabled cyber capabilities routinely to pursue geopolitical goals, with the UK facing sophisticated attacks at greater scale and speed.

The review also recorded that UK and EU member states jointly attributed a December 2025 attack on Poland's energy grid to Russia's FSB Centre 16. Had it succeeded, roughly 500,000 citizens could have lost power. Europe is not watching this threat from the sidelines; it is where the playbook is being tested.

Key Takeaways

2028 is the marker. The NCSC judges AI malware will highly likely be used in ransomware against UK CNI before the end of 2028.

Europe's grid is already a target. Russia's FSB Centre 16 was attributed to the December 2025 attack on Poland's energy grid, and a July 2026 advisory from 18 partners in 12 countries flagged the same group exploiting vulnerable routers to reach CNI networks worldwide.

China is best positioned to use AI against CNI. The NCSC rates China's activity as the most sophisticated and sustained cyber challenge facing the UK.

AI speeds up old tricks rather than inventing new ones. For large organizations, 88% of incidents the NCSC handled began through just four initial access vectors.

A "patch wave" is coming. AI-assisted vulnerability discovery will shrink the time defenders have between disclosure and exploitation.

The gap is widening. Organizations with legacy technology and slow remediation will become the preferred targets of both states and criminals.

The 2028 Warning

The NCSC's assessment is precise about where AI makes the difference. It calls AI an almost certain "force multiplier" that improves reconnaissance, social engineering, vulnerability discovery and exploit development. The biggest effect, it says, will be faster and larger versions of existing tactics rather than brand-new attack vectors.

Ransomware is where that acceleration hits CNI hardest. The review expects criminal adoption of AI to raise the scale and efficiency of ransomware, social engineering and exploitation. It also warns that open-source AI tools built for security researchers are likely to be repurposed to automate criminal workflows, cutting costs and raising attack volumes against less resilient targets.

The agency is careful not to overstate today's reality. Its Incident Management team has begun to see attackers using AI tools, but none of the observed uses enabled a new class of attack. Human operators remain essential, and the NCSC notes that losing control of an agentic AI is likely to hinder threat actors from reaching their goals.

The review's pessimistic 2028 scenario shows why that caveat may not last. In it, frontier AI is available to everyone from state actors to novice hackers, jailbroken models are sold in criminal marketplaces, and attribution becomes harder as capability spreads. It even describes a realistic possibility of an automated cyber actor operating beyond its operator's control. Cloud-controlled CNI and AI-driven robotics raise the chance that a digital compromise causes physical harm.

The NCSC stresses this is an illustration of the cost of inaction, not a forecast. But it is a scenario written by the agency responsible for defending UK infrastructure, and it is set just two years out.

Europe: The Proving Ground for CNI Attacks

If the UK is looking at 2028, continental Europe is already living with the threat. The NCSC names Russia as the most audacious cyber threat to the UK today. GCHQ Director Anne Keast-Butler goes further in the review's foreword, warning that tactics Russia developed against Ukraine are now being turned more widely on states and their institutions.

Three data points from the review frame the European picture:

Poland's energy grid (December 2025). The UK and EU member states formally attributed the attack to FSB Centre 16. If successful, it could have cut electricity to around 500,000 people.

Router exploitation on a global scale (July 2026). The NCSC and 18 international partners from 12 countries issued a joint advisory on FSB Centre 16 actors exploiting vulnerable routers to target CNI networks worldwide. On the same day, the UK sanctioned 24 individuals and entities tied to destructive cyber and hybrid operations, including criminals running proxy networks linked to Russian intelligence.

Operational technology in crosshairs. The review points to recent attacks on programmable logic controllers (PLCs) as evidence that organizations failing to modernize are falling behind.

The pattern matters for anyone running energy, water, transport or telecoms in Europe. Grids, interconnectors and supply chains cross borders, and a disruptive attack in one country can cascade into its neighbors. The review also describes how cyber threats to the UK can escalate rapidly and without warning during periods of geopolitical tension.

Add AI to this mix and the timeline compresses. A state actor that today relies on patience and known router flaws could, with AI-assisted discovery and exploitation, find and weaponize new weaknesses across thousands of European edge devices far faster than defenders can patch them.

China is Best Positioned to Turn AI on Critical Infrastructure

While Russia is the loudest threat, the NCSC sees China as the most capable. It judges that China highly likely has both the intent and the best position to use AI against CNI and other strategic targets. Its frontier AI programmes are expected to sharpen vulnerability identification, targeting efficiency and access operations.

Data sits at the center of that strategy. The review describes China collecting large volumes of information from the UK and elsewhere, then using it to train models and improve capability. In the AI era, stolen data is no longer just espionage material; it is fuel.

The UK has already acted on this. In December 2025, it sanctioned two China-based firms: i-Soon, which targeted more than 80 government and private IT systems globally, and Integrity Technology Group, which the FBI has linked to the Flax Typhoon intrusions. In April 2026, the NCSC and 15 partners across nine other countries published guidance on the covert networks most China-linked actors use to hide their activity.

The 2028 scenario adds a further concern: China, as a leading developer, may help spread advanced AI-cyber capability to other actors, letting them hide in the noise and making attribution harder for European defenders.

AI Runs the Old Playbook, Only Faster

The most useful finding in the review is also the least dramatic: attackers are still getting in through the basics. Over the past year, the NCSC received 1,831 reports of cyber attacks. Of these, 337 needed its direct support, and 80 were classed as nationally significant.

For large organizations, 88% of incidents started through four initial access vectors:

Exploiting public-facing applications

Phishing

Misuse of valid accounts

Exploiting external remote services

Even state-linked intrusions often used flaws for which patches already existed but had not been applied quickly enough. As the review puts it, sophisticated actors do not need to be sophisticated to gain initial access; their skill shows in what they do once inside.

This is exactly where AI changes the economics. The NCSC expects AI-assisted vulnerability discovery to give attackers more chances to hit systems before owners patch them. It is urging every organization to prepare for a "patch wave": a surge of security updates across the technology stack, many of them critical, as AI exposes years of technical debt.

Two further risks deserve attention:

Shadow AI. Staff moving sensitive data to personal devices to use unsanctioned AI tools leaves organizations blind to where that data goes, and open to both APT groups and criminals.

The widening gap. Mature, well-resourced organizations will use AI to detect and fix faster. Those running legacy systems will fall further behind and become more attractive targets.

The financial stakes are already clear. UK government research cited in the review puts the annual cost of malicious cyber activity to UK organizations at about £14.7 billion. The 2025 attack on Jaguar Land Rover alone cost the company around £196 million in direct costs and contributed to UK GDP growing just 0.1% in Q3 2025.

How the UK Is Fighting Back With AI

The NCSC's answer is to meet machine-speed attacks with machine-speed defense. Several initiatives in the review stand out:

Cyber Shield. A joint NCSC and DCMS programme to build a national agentic cyber defense ecosystem over five years. The NCSC supplies the platform and intelligence, while defensive agents are built by the security market and open-source community. Early phases focus on detection and blocking, where automation is already practical.

Project DROMOS. Launched in 2026 by the Government Cyber Coordination Centre and the AI Security Institute, it used frontier AI models to review government codebases. Expanded into live environments, it surfaced hundreds of potential security issues, including critical vulnerabilities.

National Detect Strategy. A pilot aiming, by 2030, to ensure defenders across critical systems can detect and respond to known vulnerabilities and attacker techniques at organizational, community and national scale.

Regulation and benchmarks. The Cyber Security and Resilience Bill brings new sectors into scope and adds national security powers. The new CAF Core Profile sets a minimum resilience baseline for essential services.

There are early results. Under the Government Cyber Action Plan, the median time to fix domain-related vulnerabilities fell from 50 days to 8. The Early Warning service now covers 19,922 organizations, up 52% on last year.

For Europe, the lesson is that partnership is now part of the defense. The review highlights the world's first AI security standard developed through ETSI, the European standards body, as proof that allies can shape AI security while the technology is still evolving.

National defense at machine speed also depends on seeing adversaries before they reach the network. Groups like FSB Centre 16 and China-linked operators plan, recruit, and trade access in places most defenders never look. As AI makes attribution harder, government agencies, national CERTs, and defense bodies need intelligence that tracks threat actors across the open, deep, and dark web and connects that activity to the infrastructure being targeted. Cyble Hawk is built for exactly this. It gives national security teams sovereign threat intelligence, adversary profiling, and investigative support. That means early warning of campaigns against critical infrastructure and stronger attribution when an attack does land. Book a demo to see how your agency can move from reacting to incidents to anticipating them.

Recommendations for CNI Operators in the UK and Europe

The NCSC's core message is that AI did not create these weaknesses; it is exposing them faster. Operators of critical infrastructure should act on the following now:

Harden the edge first. Inventory and patch internet-facing applications, VPNs, routers, and remote access services. These are the routes FSB Centre 16 and others are actively exploiting.

Prepare for the patch wave. Build processes to test and deploy security updates more often, faster and across suppliers. Track time-to-remediate as a board-level metric.

Kill password-based access where you can. Move privileged and remote users to phishing-resistant authentication such as passkeys, and audit valid accounts for misuse.

Segment IT from OT. Limit the paths from corporate networks to PLCs and industrial control systems, and monitor those boundaries continuously.

Govern AI use internally. Map what data AI tools and agents can access, what actions they can take, and how they are monitored. Close off shadow AI with approved alternatives.

Rehearse recovery, not just prevention. Test ransomware response playbooks against scenarios where operational systems must run during disruption. Use the NCSC's guidance on recovering from highly disruptive attacks.

Lock down the supply chain. Require baseline controls such as Cyber Essentials, or equivalent standards in EU frameworks, from suppliers with access to critical systems.

Use threat intelligence that moves at AI speed. Monitor for exploitation of newly disclosed flaws, stolen credentials, and chatter about your sector, so you can act before an incident escalates.

Start post-quantum planning. The NCSC wants discovery and migration planning finished by 2028, priority migrations by 2031 and full migration by 2035.

Conclusion

The NCSC has given Europe a deadline. By 2028, AI-powered ransomware against UK critical infrastructure moves from possibility to expectation, and state actors will be using AI as a routine part of their operations. The Poland grid attack and the global router campaign show the targeting is already in place; AI simply adds speed and scale.

The agency's own framing is a "moment of choice." Organizations that modernize, patch fast, and build resilience now will be able to absorb what comes next. Those that defer will find AI exposing their technical debt faster than they can repay it.

For CNI operators across the UK and Europe, the next two years are the window to close the gap. Continuous visibility into emerging vulnerabilities, active exploitation and threat actor activity will be central to staying ahead of attacks that move at machine speed.

AI-powered malware highly likely to be used in ransomware attack on Britain’s critical national infrastructure by 2028, new report warns.

Head of GCHQ’s National Cyber Security Centre to warn, as a society, the era of “tech on the cheap” at expense of security is over.

New State of the Cyber Nation report calls on organisations to make “significant changes” to avert future where AI is used against UK economy and society.

The UK’s critical national infrastructure should be braced for a ransomware attack involving AI-powered malware by 2028, a new report published today [Tuesday 3 November] by the National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) – a part of the UK’s signals intelligence agency GCHQ says.

The NCSC's State of the Cyber Nation warns that within the next two years, AI adoption by hostile actors is “highly likely” to increase the scale and efficiency of their operations, including ransomware attacks, social engineering, and vulnerability exploitation.

In a speech to launch the report, the CEO of the NCSC, Dr Richard Horne, is set to say that the AI revolution must force UK organisations to reckon with the current state of their cyber security, as new technologies will expose vulnerabilities, failings and underinvestment at an unprecedented speed and scale in the years ahead. The head of the UK's cyber agency will also set out how artificial intelligence represents the critical opportunity to improve the UK’s collective cyber resilience, but that organisations must take urgent action to address foundational investments and weaknesses or risk adversaries exploiting them instead.

The warning comes as the government is investing in the UK's defence and resilience capabilities, including greater investment in cyber defence, while taking action through the introduction of the Cyber Security and Resilience Bill and the forthcoming National Cyber Action Plan to strengthen the UK's defences, deter hostile state aggression, keep essential services running and keep the British people safe.

Alongside calls for organisations to strengthen their resilience, last week the Chancellor also announced greater investment in capabilities to help the UK harness AI for cyber defence, including £60 million into developing the first phase of a national Cyber Shield, £70 million for a new National Exposure and Real-Time Vulnerability (NERV) Centre to identify vulnerabilities across critical infrastructure and the economy, and a new AI Cyber Security Centre of Excellence, ran by the National Cyber Security Centre, in Manchester to develop world leading AI security expertise within government.

This year’s report suggests that the UK is at a point of “enormous consequence” for cyber security and that organisations across the UK must make use of the tools, standards and frameworks that already exist and are evidenced to protect them from conventional and AI-powered cyber attacks.

The NCSC is imploring organisations across the UK to face what Dr Horne is calling “a moment of choice”. In a speech to launch the report, NCSC CEO is expected to say:

In the coming months, we face a real prospect of an unprecedented rise in the number of cyber incidents. But we must be clear that is not because AI has invented new ways to attack us. But because vulnerabilities that have been tolerated for far too long can now be discovered and exploited at a scale that was once unimaginable.

“For decades, we have collectively got away with doing tech on the cheap.

“We can be a nation where leaders of all organisations actively choose to invest with urgency... And where all organisations make security and resilience a fundamental requirement, not an afterthought.

“The collective result would be a source of enduring national strength for us all.

Dr Horne will urge all organisations across the country to “take the responsibility now to make different choices”, including addressing the failure to adequately invest in their technology; not having technology unnecessarily connected to the internet; and making Cyber Essentials the starting point for cyber security, not the end goal, with organisations building greater resilience according to their size, complexity and risk.

He will say that failing to make these choices will result in leaders “having to look their investors, shareholders, employees, customers, suppliers, in the eye and explain...when food isn’t on shelves, lights aren’t on, businesses have gone under.”

In their tenth year, the National Cyber Security Centre plays a more important role than ever before, defending our security on the cyber frontline.

“The NCSC's latest annual report shows cyber threats are growing more sophisticated. We're using the power of AI to help stay ahead of those who seek to do us harm, with a new national Cyber Shield and an AI Cyber Security Centre of Excellence.

AI-powered malware is strongly expected to feature in ransomware attacks on the UK’s critical national infrastructure by 2028, the country’s National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) has warned.

The country faces “a real prospect of an unprecedented rise in the number of cyber incidents,” NCSC CEO Richard Horne said during the launch event for the agency’s annual State of the Cyber Nation report in London, on November 3.

Horne said this heightened threat is supercharged by the use of AI, whose impact “will be felt by us all, whether you and your organization choose to harness it or not.”

The report warned that AI-powered malicious software is “highly likely” to be used in cyber-attacks conducted by financially motivated hackers against the UK’s power stations, airports and hospitals by 2028.

It also warned that nation states including Russia and China will routinely use AI in their cyber activity to achieve their geopolitical goals.

Yet, Horne emphasized that AI-based threats have not fundamentally revealed anything new.

The risk that looms is “not because AI has invented new ways to attack us,” he argued, but “because vulnerabilities that have been tolerated for far too long can now be discovered and exploited at a scale that was once unimaginable.”

He pointed to “far too many organizations” relying on “tech on the cheap.”

“End-of-life systems kept running for just one more year, well-needed upgrades pushed back, as a 'cost efficiency' and technology providers failing to invest in security by design and default,” Horne outlined.

“We have installed technology then failed to invest in it throughout its lifecycle. Granted access where it was convenient rather than where it was necessary. Procured services based solely on their price without asking whether the technologies and operations underpinning them was resilient or secure. And failed to put in place the monitoring needed to detect when things go wrong,” he added.

UK Government Announces New Cybersecurity Investments

The best recent example, Horne said, is the threat of the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities. He noted that his agency has issued 110,000 proactive notifications and Early Warning alerts to UK organizations in response to the PHP vulnerabilities.

He also welcomed recent news that the British government has invested £60m ($80.4m) into developing the first phase of a national Cyber Shield, including a £25m ($33.5m) Challenge Fund supporting UK AI and cyber security innovators, and £70m ($93.8m) for a new National Exposure and Real-Time Vulnerability (NERV) Centre.

These announcements, made on October 24, come alongside an additional £120m ($160.8m) investment in the AI Security Institute (AISI) and the establishment of new AI Cyber Security Centre of Excellence, ran by the NCSC in Manchester to provide world leading AI security expertise within government.

The government has also committed £40m ($53.6m) to establishing a National Agentic Security Unit to monitor and respond to uncontrolled AI bots, alongside a further £24m ($32.1m) to strengthen public-sector cyber defenses using advanced AI technology.

Alongside these investments, Cyber Security Minister, Baroness Lloyd, announced in a speech at the NCSC Annual Review event that the UK government is offering a 75% discount on Cyber Essentials certification for micro, small and medium-sized businesses, bringing the cost down to between £80 ($107) and £125 ($168), plus VAT.

More than 230 businesses have also signed up to the government's Cyber Resilience Pledge, which will allow participating organizations to refer SMEs in their supply chains for free Cyber Essentials certification, with selected businesses also receiving support from a free cyber security advisor.

The government also announced 14 new Software Security Ambassadors, including Fortinet, Thales, Capgemini and Zscaler, which will work with the government to promote secure software development and encourage wider adoption of its Software Security Code of Practice.

A “Moment of Choice” for UK Organizations

Horne said UK organizations and at “a moment of choice” and urged them to “reckon with the current state of their cybersecurity” as new technologies like AI will expose vulnerabilities, failings and underinvestment at an unprecedented speed and scale in the years ahead.

The NCSC report also suggested that the UK is at a point of “enormous consequence” for cybersecurity and that organizations must make use of the tools, standards and frameworks that already exist and are evidenced to protect them from conventional and AI-powered cyber-attacks.

"We can be a nation where leaders of all organizations actively choose to invest with urgency and where all organizations make security and resilience a fundamental requirement, not an afterthought. The collective result would be a source of enduring national strength for us all,” Horne said in his speech.

He added that failing to make these choices will result in leaders “having to look their investors, shareholders, employees, customers, suppliers, in the eye and explain, when food isn’t on shelves, lights aren’t on, businesses have gone under.”

Commenting on the report, Anthony Young, CEO at UK-based critical infrastructure security provider Bridewell, stressed that the NCSC’s two-year warning “feels generous.”

“AI is already helping attackers, and vulnerability discovery is accelerating faster than many organizations can test and deploy patches. There is no time to wait when so many of the weaknesses attackers can exploit are already there, highlighting the recent attacks on supermarket refrigeration systems are a good example of this and “an extension of the problems we have seen for years with internet-connected CCTV and heating or ventilation systems.”

“Organizations cannot assume that insurance will resolve the consequences of an attack when essential services are disrupted. Cyber Essentials matters because so many attacks still exploit basic weaknesses, and leaving those weaknesses in place makes life too easy for everyone from amateur hackers to nation-state attackers. We’ve spent 25 years telling organisations to get the basics right. AI is making it harder for them to get away with ignoring that advice,” Young added.

The warnings come as the UK government is taking action through the introduction of the Cyber Security and Resilience Bill and the forthcoming National Cyber Action Plan to strengthen the UK's defenses.

Singapore’s Cybersecurity Code of Practice for Critical Information Infrastructure 2026 marks an important shift in how CII owners must think about security.

The focus is no longer limited to protecting the designated CII environment itself. CCoP 2026 places greater emphasis on Board and senior-management accountability, visibility into systems connected to CII, continuous monitoring, behavioural baselining, threat hunting and evidence that security controls are working as intended.

For security leaders, the challenge is clear: attackers do not respect organisational or network boundaries.

The attack path extends beyond the CII environment

An attacker may first compromise a user account, remote-access system, engineering workstation or management server before moving toward the systems that deliver essential services.

CCoP 2026 reflects this reality by extending security requirements beyond the designated CII itself. The Code distinguishes between enterprise systems, CII interconnected systems, and the CII systems that deliver essential services, with new Section 12 requirements focused specifically on systems that connect to or communicate with CII.

This means CII organisations need more than a static view of what should exist. They need to understand what is communicating, how identities and systems are behaving, and whether suspicious activity is progressing toward critical infrastructure.

Where Vectra AI can support CCoP readiness

Vectra AI supports CII organisations in the areas where visibility, detection, investigation, and response are most important.

“CCoP 2026 reflects today’s evolving threats to critical infrastructure. Vectra AI supports 31 of the 38 clauses relevant to its capabilities within the Code’s 53 clauses, helping organisations detect threats earlier and respond before critical operations are disrupted.”

— Hock Leng, Vice President of Sales, APJ, Vectra AI

See what is communicating with CII

Based on our clause-by-clause assessment of CCoP 2026, Vectra AI directly or supportively aligns with 31 of the Code’s 53 clauses. That alignment is strongest across visibility, monitoring and detection, threat hunting, incident response, OT monitoring and interconnected-system security. Alignment does not mean Vectra AI alone satisfies each clause, but that its capabilities can directly support or strengthen the required control.

Detect abnormal behaviour earlier

Section 6.2 requires CIIOs to establish normal operational and network activity, monitor deviations, correlate cybersecurity events, and trigger alerts for investigation. The Code also recognises that attackers may use less-monitored areas as stepping stones toward CII.

This aligns closely with Vectra AI’s core capabilities. The platform analyses activity across network, identity and cloud environments to identify abnormal behaviour, correlate related events, and prioritise the entities that present the greatest risk.

Instead of presenting analysts with disconnected alerts, Vectra AI helps show how an attack is progressing and what requires immediate attention.

Support threat hunting, investigation and response

CCoP also places greater emphasis on proactive threat hunting and incident readiness.

Vectra AI provides enriched metadata, behavioural context, and investigation workflows that help analysts search for hidden activity, reconstruct attack paths, and determine whether a cybersecurity incident is underway.

When response is required, integrations can support native actions such as isolating a host, restricting a compromised account, or blocking malicious traffic. These capabilities strengthen the technical execution of incident response, while the CIIO retains ownership of its response plan, regulatory reporting, forensics, and recovery processes.

Supporting OT and interconnected environments

Many CII environments include OT, legacy systems, and devices that cannot support endpoint agents.

Vectra AI can passively monitor visible traffic in these environments without requiring agents on sensitive systems. This is particularly relevant to the requirement in Section 10.2 to monitor OT-to-enterprise data flows for anomalies, as well as Section 12.7 requirements to investigate suspicious activity across interconnected systems.

Additional controls are still required for areas such as endpoint logs, virtualisation infrastructure, patching and formal reporting to CSA, but Vectra AI can provide an important layer of behavioural visibility across the communication paths attackers may use.

Start with the visibility gap

For CII organisations preparing for CCoP 2026, a practical starting point is to ask:

Do we know every system that communicates with the CII?

Can we detect when a valid identity or trusted system begins behaving abnormally?

Can we show what the security team saw, investigated, and did in response?

Vectra AI does not replace the governance, certification, IAM, patching, backup or regulatory-reporting controls required by CCoP. Its role is to help CII organisations see attacker behaviour earlier, investigate faster and produce stronger operational evidence that their detection and response controls are working.

articles.title: Whole-of-state defense: How SLED agencies can secure critical infrastructure in the AI era
articles.context: The NASCIO-GDIT brief cites emerging threats such as automated reconnaissance, and it urges states to prepare for an increase in AI-enabled attacks on critical infrastructure,...
articles.full_text:
AI is widening the attack surface of the critical infrastructure facilities and services that state, local, and education (SLED) organizations run. In the final post of our Cybersecurity Awareness Month series, we explain how a whole-of-state security approach can help SLED agencies protect their critical infrastructure.

Key takeaways

Because cyber attackers prey on under-resourced targets, they often go after SLED organizations, especially those that operate critical infrastructure, including water systems, hospitals, mass transit, emergency services, and schools.

In the latest research from the National Association of State Chief Information Officers (NASCIO), nearly 90% of state CIOs rated cyberattacks on critical systems as a high concern.

AI expands the attack surface in two fundamental ways: SLED agencies and employees adopt AI tools and AI-built apps faster than security teams can authorize and inventory them, while attackers use AI automation to find weak points faster.

A whole-of-state cybersecurity approach treats state agencies, counties, cities, school districts, and utilities as one defensive perimeter, with shared visibility, shared services, and clear governance.

Cyber attackers often look for the weakest link that can offer them an entry point into larger targets. If they can’t crack a state agency’s hardened systems, they’ll try to breach it in a roundabout way by first breaking into a small town’s water utility, a rural school district, or a county dispatch center, and then attempt to move laterally toward the bigger target.

When one of those weak links fails, the consequences can reach well beyond the breached agency: halted 911 dispatches, disrupted water service, exposed resident data, and more.

AI is further complicating the picture.

State, local, and education (SLED) organizations are adopting AI quickly to improve efficiency, employees are building applications with it informally, and adversaries are using it to speed up reconnaissance. Each of those developments is making it harder for security teams to protect SLED agencies.

In this fourth and final blog in our Cybersecurity Awareness Month series, we focus on what that expanding AI attack surface means for state, local, and education cybersecurity leaders responsible for critical infrastructure, and how whole-of-state cybersecurity can help them stay ahead.

Why SLED critical infrastructure is a prime target

SLED organizations operate critical infrastructure, such as water treatment plants, transportation systems, public hospitals, schools, and emergency communications, across many of the 16 critical infrastructure sectors categorized by the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA).

State technology leaders are concerned about protecting these critical infrastructure facilities and services from cyber attacks, as “The Expanding Cyber Perimeter” report, published in September by the National Association of State Chief Information Officers (NASCIO) and General Dynamics Information Technology (GDIT), found.

Here are five key findings from the report, which drew on the 2026 NASCIO State CIO Survey, the 2026 NASCIO-Deloitte Cybersecurity Study, and interviews with state CISOs:

Nearly 90% of state CIOs rate cyber attacks on critical systems as a high concern. The rest rate them as moderate.

State CIOs report low confidence in local governments’ cyber practices. The report’s authors also say it’s unclear how states should help local governments and independent local government entities, like special districts.

Water and wastewater plants, dams, hospitals, and transportation services face the greatest cyber risk.

Many systems run on aging or proprietary operational technology (OT) with no upgrade path, and broad remote access increases their cyber risk.

Small communities and special districts often have limited cyber staff, aging equipment, and complex OT with few controls. With hundreds of such entities in a single state, attackers have plenty of entry points to try.

Responsibility is also murky. According to the NASCIO-GDIT report, it’s often unclear which agency is responsible for responding to an attack on critical infrastructure, especially where legal authority, governance, or partnerships aren’t in place.

Cyber risk extends beyond technical and geographical boundaries. When an attacker breaches systems of a county water utility or a school district, the incident can have widespread consequences.

State and local officials and their CIOs and CISOs should stop treating these incidents as one city’s or one county’s problem. Robert Beach, then CTO of the City of Cocoa, Florida, and a member of the Multi-State Information Sharing and Analysis Center (MS-ISAC) executive committee, told StateScoop last year that an attack on critical infrastructure “is an attack on the nation.”

Insiders add another layer of risk. Another MS-ISAC report, “Strengthening Critical Infrastructure: SLTT Progress & Priorities,” published in August 2025, flagged excessive access to system controls as a vulnerability. The report recommended agencies review who can reach their networks and disable credentials promptly when employees leave.

The 2026 NASCIO-Deloitte study underscores the risk, noting that attackers exploit compromised credentials and former employee accounts, so regular access reviews and prompt offboarding remain essential.

Recent cyber attacks against water systems have made the threat very real. On July 30, the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) and the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) warned that water and wastewater sector utilities in at least seven states had reported cyber attacks, leading in some cases to degraded water operations.

That same day, the CISA said it had observed “a significant increase in cyber threat actors targeting programmable logic controllers” in the water and wastewater sector.

“Threat actors targeting exposed PLCs have modified passwords to lock out operators and disconnected the PLCs by changing their IP addresses. This activity has resulted in boil water notices and sustained manual operations,” the CISA alert reads.

A week earlier, CISA and several federal agencies had published a joint advisory warning critical infrastructure organizations in the government, water, and energy sectors of “ongoing cyber exploitation of internet-connected OT devices.”

Tenable researchers recommend removing internet-exposed PLCs and setting their mode switches to “Run”, among other steps. The U.S. government is also tightening cybersecurity regulations for water and wastewater utilities.

Federal and state leaders are mobilizing, too.

In August, Texas Governor Greg Abbott, National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross, and Texas Cyber Command Chief Vice Admiral (Ret.) TJ White launched Project Watershed at a roundtable in San Antonio, Texas, which I was honored to attend. Project Watershed is a joint effort aimed at strengthening the cybersecurity of Texas water and wastewater systems against threats from hostile foreign adversaries.

Governor Abbott said that through the project, “our communities and water systems will be better secured from the onslaught of cyber-attacks.”

Protecting the water systems Americans rely on every day is a shared responsibility, and Project Watershed shows the kind of public-private collaboration a whole-of-state approach depends on.

How AI expands the attack surface

AI has moved from pilot project to operational reality in state government. NASCIO’s 2026 research shows AI overtaking cybersecurity as the top policy priority for state CIOs, the first time in more than a decade that cybersecurity loses the top spot.

AI adoption is good news for service delivery, but it also increases SLED agencies’ cyber risk. Three forces drive the rise in cyber risk:

Employees build and adopt AI tools on their own. As we covered earlier in this series, non-technical staff can now use AI tools to generate working applications using natural-language prompts, often without permission from the IT and security departments. In a government setting, those unsanctioned apps can access resident data, case management systems, and internal credentials, all without testing, patching, or monitoring.

AI shows up inside the software SLED agencies already own, as vendors quietly add AI features and connectors to their products, which can expand data access and permissions without the awareness of the IT and security teams.

Attackers use automation to move faster. The NASCIO-GDIT brief cites emerging threats such as automated reconnaissance, and it urges states to prepare for an increase in AI-enabled attacks on critical infrastructure, as the window between when an exposure appears and when attackers exploit it keeps shrinking.

For critical infrastructure operators, the stakes rise further. Their aging OT systems with broad remote access are already a soft target. Unvetted AI apps, over-permissioned connectors, and automated scanning by attackers quickly multiply the number of paths an attacker can chain together.

The key for SLED agency CISOs is to see their exposures across IT, OT, cloud, identity, and AI as one connected picture, and to prioritize and act on the ones an attacker could realistically exploit to reach systems that matter to public safety. An exposure management program can help SLED agencies address this cyber risk with comprehensive visibility, prioritization, and AI-assisted action.

What a whole-of-state approach looks like

A whole-of-state approach treats state agencies, local governments, schools, and utilities as one defensive perimeter instead of a collection of individual, siloed organizations.

The state government should share governance frameworks, visibility of IT/OT assets and security findings, and cybersecurity capabilities so the smallest entity doesn’t have to defend itself alone.

As Tenable’s Matt Kucik explains in the blog, “Whole-of-state cybersecurity: Uniting SLED agencies for maximum impact,” success starts with leadership and vision, open communication, and an actionable plan.

The model is gaining ground. The NASCIO-GDIT report found that 73% of states responding to the 2026 State CIO Survey include critical infrastructure cyber protection in their whole-of-state plans. It calls these models the main framework emerging for statewide resilience. Maturity varies widely, though. Four building blocks separate strong programs from weak ones:

Governance and clear roles. CISA’s state cybersecurity governance case studies highlight Georgia and Virginia, which use formal structures to treat cyber risk as a collective priority. They have proactively defined who is in charge of prevention, who is in charge of responding, and who is in charge of generating incident reports.

Shared visibility. You can’t prioritize what you can’t see. A statewide view of assets and exposures lets a small water district benefit from the same insight as a large state agency.

Shared services. In Utah, its federally funded shared services program offers endpoint protection, patching, training, and incident response to roughly 80% of local government entities in the state. The state secured an additional $1.5 million for water-sector cybersecurity.

Trust earned through results. What local partners need from the state is faster remediation, lower costs, and fewer surprises. New Jersey CISO Michael Geraghty made this point in the NASCIO-GDIT report: Telling local governments you’re from the state and here to help doesn’t earn their trust. Results do.

It’s also key to share information quickly. Terry Loftus, CIO of the San Diego County Office of Education and an MS-ISAC committee member, told StateScoop that many districts learn of attacks when they receive a ransomware demand.

State cybersecurity agencies should build channels that proactively push threat intelligence and exposure data to every entity in their state, to increase the chances of preventing attacks.

Five steps SLED agencies can take to boost their cyber defenses

Here’s Tenable’s advice on where to start, whether you lead a state agency, a county IT shop, a school district, or a municipal utility:

Create and continuously update a complete inventory of your critical infrastructure assets, including OT systems, remote access paths, and AI tools and apps. Start with the systems that affect public health and safety.

Prioritize by exploitability and impact. Don’t chase every finding. Focus on the exposures an attacker could realistically chain together to reach water, power, health, or emergency systems. Removing internet-exposed controllers and securing any remote access paths to them should be the highest priority.

Share visibility across jurisdictions. Give small entities access to the same insight larger agencies have, whether through statewide tooling, shared services, or regular information-sharing forums.

Govern AI use before it sprawls. Set clear policies, approved-tool lists, and training for employees who build with AI.

Check if State and Local Cybersecurity Grant Program (SLCGP) funding is still available in your state to help fund these priorities.

How Tenable can help SLED agencies

Tenable One OT Exposure capabilities extend that visibility, insight, and action to the OT and extended internet of things (xIoT) devices used by many critical infrastructure organizations.

With Tenable One, SLED teams can see what they have, understand which exposures matter most, and take prioritized actions, maximizing staff and grant dollars to drive down cyber risk.

The City of Raleigh in North Carolina, for example, uses Tenable to ensure the safety and sustainability of its public water systems. To see how Tenable supports statewide programs, explore our state, local, and education solutions and learn how Tenable helps meet SLCGP requirements.

Looking ahead

The attack surface is growing, a trend that AI is accelerating. Federal funding is shrinking, and its future is uncertain. Yet the fundamentals of resilience stay the same: know your assets, understand your exposures, share what you learn, and act together before an attacker forces your hand.

No single state or jurisdiction has solved this, and no single tool will. A whole-of-state approach gives SLED organizations the best chance to stay ahead of the threats facing the critical services residents rely on every day.
